Mr. Speaker,
I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, involving the security and confidentiality of tax and statistical data supplied by Canadians in trust to their government.
Since it has been demonstrated that tax and statistical information has been left open to public inspection, and that the responsibility rests with the cabinet and particularly with the departments of National Revenue and Industry, Trade and Commerce, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY RECOMMENDED BY SCIENCE COUNCIL-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce-who are probably discussing whether the Prime Minister was sinful or not by going south-I have a question for the president of the economic board of refugees.
First, I want to know whether the minister has examined the study "Forging the Links," of the Science Council of Canada. If so, does he have a comment on the situation they describe on page 17 "as a massive failure of the country's industrial system", that imports have grown from 26 per cent to 31 per
Oral Questions
cent of our Canadian market-that imports grew to 31 per cent up to 1977-and our exports are declining relatively, and that we are moving from an industrialized economy to one based on the export of raw materials?
Has the minister studied this report? Did he read it before he stated and came to the decision that Canada should have no coherent industrial strategy which the Science Council of Canada recommends?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development
subsubtopic: INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY RECOMMENDED BY SCIENCE COUNCIL-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is, again, making distortions out of any comments I made. Yes, the report to which he referred is a matter of very important significance to the government. It is being studied most carefully.
With regard to the question of imports, the hon. member might be interested to know that in the last two years the growth of import penetration in Canada is the smallest of 11 OECD countries, which is a source of some comfort to us.
With regard to the development of industrial strategies, we have been, and will continue to be, diligent in working toward that end.

subsubtopic: INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY RECOMMENDED BY SCIENCE COUNCIL-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
I realize the minister is being diligent, Mr. Speaker, but he has not come up with any industrial strategies that the Science Council of Canada know about. The Prime Minister said to help him, he is in trouble, but we want Canada helped because Canada is in trouble as a result of this ten years of inaction.
Would the minister comment on page 24 of the report where the Science Council deals with the question of invisible trade, items such as transport services, tourism, investment income and payment on the debt which has risen, by the way, from $1.5 billion in interest on our foreign debt to $4.8 billion which is estimated this year-and it will be worse in the future. They state that of 25 industrial countries, Canada is twenty-fifth in the contribution of invisible trade items to our trade account.
Will the minister tell the House whether he has now developed any strategy in dealing with this desparate situation, other than the strategy of borrowing $8 billion or $9 billion abroad to add to that tremendous deficit? What is his strategy for dealing with this?

subsubtopic: INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY RECOMMENDED BY SCIENCE COUNCIL-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member is referring to the deficit in the current account. I have, of course, said that we have a current account deficit that is quite significant in Canada. Traditionally, we have opted for investment from abroad.
Canada is a country that has been developing over the past 110 years through borrowing from abroad. We are, in fact, a developing nation with a lot of infrastructure to put in place. It has been traditional for Canada to borrow abroad. Therefore, that is what we are doing at this time. I think this policy has served Canada very well for a long time.

subsubtopic: INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY RECOMMENDED BY SCIENCE COUNCIL-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister has not answered my question. I will ask his deskmate, the President of the

February 26, 1979
Oral Questions
Board of Economic Development Ministers-who is now supposed to head this area-what specific policies the government is developing to overcome this tremendous deficit on the invisible trade account, particularly in view of the fact that the study has found that in the sectors of our manufacturing which utilize high technology, we are in a very serious deficit situation and our surplus in exports is really from raw materials and crude and processed resource material.
In view of this, what are the minister's promises? His deskmate is borrowing billions more abroad and there will be very much higher interest payments. How is the minister going to overcome that on the trade surplus or the surplus side of our international balance of accounts? If not, the Canadian dollar is doomed to even worse decreases. What is his answer to this?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development
subsubtopic: INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY RECOMMENDED BY SCIENCE COUNCIL-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the greatest dangers to the Canadian dollar is spurious comments like that of the hon. member and some of his colleagues. There is a great deal of encouragement to be taken from the increase in our export merchandise trade balance which will reach $3.5 billion this year with every sign, over and above the advantage the Canadian dollar gives us for exports these days, of a vast improvement in the competitive position of Canadian manufacturing. That fact is well known to the manufacturing industry and is a matter of their comments in recent consultations and public statements by them.
I really believe the hon. member would serve the country much better if he would give some kind of hope based on facts that are well known and well established. If he wants to deal in facts of three or four years ago and peddle those across the country, he is not encouraging optimism or investor confidence in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I should also like to direct my question to the minister in charge of the BED ministers of this cabinet: it centres on the question of an industrial strategy.
Does the minister agree with his counterpart, the President of the Treasury Board, that it is not the quantum of national debt that worries him but, rather, the amount of interest we are paying on it? I ask this question bearing in mind that just before this government took power, the total interest portion of the national budget was about 9 per cent, compared to 16.5 per cent now.

Mr. Speaker, this question was handled by the President of the Treasury Board quite efficiently last week when he explained to Canadians that, of course, we have a large debt in Canada but that in relation to what the debt was in 1962 in terms of percentage of gross national product, the proportion of Canadian debt at this time has dropped from 30 per cent to 23 per cent, and that is a good achievement.
[Mr. Crosbic.J

Mr. Speaker, if the minister in charge of the BED ministers does not wish to reply, perhaps I could put my supplementary question to the Minister of Finance, the minister who has attempted to justify the $62 billion net debt of this country at the present time.
Following the pattern set in the United States and in the United Kingdom, will the minister give us a five-year overview in relation to expenditure and revenue figures in Canada with a view to establishing what, in fact, will be the borrowing needs of this government this year and for the ensuing four years, bearing in mind that Wood Gundy points out that the total borrowing requirement of this government for this year and the next four years will amount to $55 billion?
I would like the minister first to indicate whether he confirms this five-year forecast and, second, will he confirm that $55 billion is, in fact, the amount the government will likely be borrowing if its plans are carried out?

Mr. Speaker, each year we table before the House a budget which includes the government's expenditures and revenue. We are fully aware that the service of our debt is presently quite costly and that our requirements for liquid assets of $10.7 billion are very high. That is why over the last three years we have undertaken to cut back our expenses, and I am certain that the hon. member will agree with me that our deficit should not increase; also I hope that he will not endorse the statements made by his leader who has gone across Canada recommending tax cuts that would increase the deficit by $6 to $7 billion next year.

subsubtopic: REASON FOR INCREASES IN FOOD PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
On the weekend, the Anti-Inflation Board produced figures showing that food prices went up a full 21 per cent over last year. In view of the fact that this is the biggest increase in the history of indexing, and considering that this process is continuing day after day, will the minister explain why flour prices-which affect the price of so many food items, including bread-have gone up, according to the same report, by a full 25 per cent in the past two months, when the removal of the federal subsidy should have meant a price increase much lower than that?

speakeroldname: Hon. Warren Allmand (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: REASON FOR INCREASES IN FOOD PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to the AIB report, the reason for food price increases is, as we have been stating all along, the increase in the price of beef, fresh fruits and vegetables and of bakery products.
February 26, 1979

The increase in the price of fruits and vegetables in part is due to the difference in the value of our dollar and the American dollar, particularly during the winter when these commodities are imported. The increase in the price of beef, as is well known, relates to the beef cycle. We have been trying to encourage people to move to alternatives to beef, especially pork, the price of which has been very good in recent weeks.
On the question of flour and bakery products, we estimated that the removal of the subsidy should result in an additional cost of seven cents on a standard loaf of bread. I have not been able to analyse the figures with respect to flour. I think the hon. member referred to bakery flour, and I would have to analyse the figures which he gave and of which I have not had notice. However, I will be pleased to do that and get back to him.

subsubtopic: REASON FOR INCREASES IN FOOD PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as usual, the minister is going to set up another study to investigate some price increase. It would be nice for him to come to the House just for once having conducted an investigation of the matter about which he is almost certain to be asked.
The Anti-Inflation Board also confirmed at the weekend that chicken retail prices went up some 35 per cent in the past year, more than twice as much as the farmer received. Since this question was raised with the minister in the House by one of my colleagues more than a week ago, will he now confirm that in the case of chicken prices the middlemen simply increased their profits on chickens by increasing chicken prices to correspond with beef price increases, even though there were not real increases in the cost of chicken production to correspond with increases in the cost of producing beef?
If there is profiteering in this area-and all the evidence seems to indicate that there is-will the minister do something such as rolling back price increases for chicken?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is very easy for the hon. member to come to the House every day to ask questions without giving notice. I have pages and pages of briefing here on food price increases, but the hon. member always manages to come up with some obscure question.

As the hon. member knows, there are marketing boards for chicken and turkey, and we hope measures will be taken to

increase quotas for those two items so that there will be a greater supply and, therefore, a lowering of prices.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice. Since the beginning of this session, I have been intrigued by the sight, at the west door of parliament, of a person walking about holding a sign. As that sign was unilingual, I could not make out too well what was written on it. Last week I went to the person and asked her: Are we not in a bilingual country: why could your

sign not be bilingual? The next day I had the pleasant surprise of seeing that it was bilingual. I could then better understand her claims. I should like to ask the Minister of Justice whether, in that capacity, he would be willing, or has already done so, to look into the claims of that person who is still there despite the very cold weather and whether he could tell us very frankly after having met her what the position of the government is with regard to her situation and, if she has certain rights, how he could help her to make herself heard democratically in order to settle that matter once and for all?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. Unfortunately, I must tell the hon. member that this person is complaining about the decision brought down by the Quebec Court of Appeal confirming the judgment of the Quebec Superior Court. As the right hon. Prime Minister mentioned in the House last week or two weeks ago, I believe, our examination of the case has shown that there is nothing we can do as a government. The case resulted from a matter under municipal jurisdiction, more specifically that of the city of Hull; we must respect the decisions of the courts just like any other Canadian citizen is expected to do. So, despite my conversations with that lady and our examination of the case, I feel there is nothing we can do as a government because to do otherwise would be tantamount to intervening in the decisions of our tribunals. subsubtopic: OPPORTUNITY TO INTRODUCE BILL TO ESTABLISH OMBUDSMAN AT FEDERAL LEVEL
speechtext:

February 26, 1979

first place, concerning complaints of citizens about administration of justice, as in the present case, the complaint would not have to be filed with the ombudsman but with the Canadian Judicial Council which, as far as I know, has considered the matter and found that there was no ground for complaint. subsubtopic: REQUEST PROCEEDINGS OF HOUSE BE BROADCAST EARLIER IN DAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Communications. subsubtopic: REQUEST PROCEEDINGS OF HOUSE BE BROADCAST EARLIER IN DAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at the present time the debates of the House of Commons are broadcast mainly on community channels, and only people in the Ottawa area have direct access to the live broadcasting of those debates. As for the province of Quebec and the debates of the National Assembly, Radio-Quebec is responsible for that broadcast. Consequently it has the choice to have a live broadcast in some areas of Quebec. As far as our debates are concerned, we can only have a pre-recorded broadcast outside the Ottawa area. The problem is quite different in a large country like ours but CBC is taking steps to broadcast the debates by satellite. On their side, cable TV companies are taking steps to broadcast the debates and in a few days, a workshop will be held to try to come up with a package which could be programmed by satellite, which would enable a larger number of people to see a live broadcast of the debates.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: TRAGEDY IN MINE AT GLACE BAY, N.S.-INVESTIGATION BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to join with the expression of sympathy in the motion under Standing Order 43 moved by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond and express my sympathy to the families who have suffered the loss or severe injury of loved ones in that tragic accident.
Today I appointed Mr. Roy Elfstrom, the director of the occupational safety and health branch of my department, as a commissioner with powers under the Inquiries Act to do an immediate on-the-spot investigation into the causes of the accident so far as they can be determined. Already a preliminary investigation is under way which is being conducted on a tripartite basis, that is, safety officers from Labour Canada who are in Sydney all the time, members of the unions involved, and of the company.
I felt it was necessary to make a second inquiry in order to secure all physical evidence and if necessary all testimony under oath before physical evidence changes or people's memories slip. Also, I am giving consideration, although I have not reached a decision, to appointing a public inquiry should that seem to be necessary.

speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subsubtopic: COMMEMORATIVE CEREMONIES TO MARK D-DAY LANDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, June 6, 1979, marks the thirty-fifth anniversary of the D-Day landings in Normandy. I would like at this time to pay homage to the gallant Canadian sailors, soldiers and airmen who took part in the allied invasion of Normandy on June 6, 1944, the greatest amphibious operation of all time.
Thousands of Canadians servicemen in the Canadian 3rd division, 2nd Canadian armoured brigade and 1st Canadian parachute battalion-nearly one-fifth of the total invasion force of 100,000 men-stormed across the Normandy beaches and elsewhere to free northwest Europe from the tyranny of enemy occupation. By the end of that dramatic day 35 years ago, it had become apparent that the massive venture had succeeded, though it represented for Canada a loss of 1,074 killed, wounded and missing.
Canadian veterans of the three services who took part in the Normandy landings continue to reflect on those events and think of their comrades who fell, denied the chance to return home and partake of the opportunities of our growing and prosperous land.
This coming June, Mr. Speaker, I will lead a delegation of 40 veterans, representing the Canadian units, battalions, regiments and corps which took part in Operation Overlord. Commemorative ceremonies will be held at Beny-sur-Mer and other sites in the Canadian sector. The group will also participate in British and American ceremonies in the respective sectors. Representatives of the Royal Canadian Legion and National Council of Veterans Associations will also attend these commemorative ceremonies.
I must remind hon. members that we emerged as a great nation because of the tens of thousands of young men and women-including some who sit here today as members of parliament-who volunteered in two world wars to fight for their country in far off lands when our freedom was threatened. These Canadians served and fought together, regardless of language, race or color. They fought united as Canadians on the Normandy beaches and later in the campaign in northwest Europe-the final turning point in the titanic struggle to preserve freedom and democracy in the world.
Let us remember today and always the thousands of Canadians who lie in graves in France and around the world because of their duty to Canada. They, by their sacrifice, protected our freedom to govern and to build a great nation for those of us who remain. They have earned their place of honour, and "We will remember them".

speechtext: Hear, hear!

The minister is quite correct in terming this the greatest amphibious opera-

tion of all times and no one who lived through those days will ever forget the fear and tension of the moment.
It is also important that Canadians not yet born in 1944 be reminded of the valiant efforts of the invasion force and the terrible losses suffered during that day-1,074 killed, wounded and missing in a single day. The figure is awesome.
I congratulate the minister on his plan to lead a delegation of veterans who took part in Operation Overlord to the commemorative ceremonies at Beny-sur-Mer. I am sure this will be a moving occasion for all involved and will serve to draw special attention to the thirty-fifth anniversary of D-Day.

I am thinking particularly of veterans who were accorded veterans' preference in employment in the public service and who are now suffering from an apparent change of government policy in this regard. I also refer to veterans experiencing difficulties obtaining admission to former veterans' hospitals, widows of veterans denied a pension because of the government's failure to act on the recommendations of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs relating to prisoners of war, war amputees and others.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, by all means let us remember the anniversary of the D-Day landings in Normandy; but at the same time let this government manifest in a tangible way to the veterans of this country that they are remembered also.

You will have a lot of him later. The government, in the words of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), believes that housing is a luxury and will always be considered a luxury. I can only relate the facts of the latest available study, including all of the ones I have from the minister's own office.
More than 40 per cent of Canadian home owners had personal incomes in 1976 of less than $10,000 and 67 per cent of them had incomes under $15,000-and the government think that mortgage deductibility is just for the rich. Less than 6 per cent of all Canadian home owners reported personal incomes of more than $25,000 in 1976. If one takes household income, which is the total income in a household, even if more than one spouse works or there are working dependants, the figures for 1976 show that 35 per cent of all home owners in Canada had an income under $10,000 a year. Slightly more than 10 per cent of all Canadian home owners recorded household incomes of more than $25,000.
These are the facts about Canadian home owners who the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) claim are too rich to deserve any kind of tax break from their government in Ottawa. In terms of occupation, it is worth noting that the largest single category of homeowners, almost 35 per cent, are skilled or unskilled labourers. When we get out on the hustings, Mr. Speaker, I wonder what the other two parties are prepared to do, and will they go into the union halls and factories and tell these Canadians that they are too well off to warrant a tax reduction?
What about the second largest category of home owners? They are retired people and account for 19 per cent of all home owners. Are they the rich?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND

Well, tell that to the home owners. Tell them they should not have a tax break. In fact, these classified home owners, the top income category, account for little more than 6 per cent of all Canadian home owners. The minister spent most of his time last Friday discussing the benefits of extending tax reductions to the beleaguered Canadian home owner. Like a variety of economists, columnists and politicians who

criticize our proposal, it has been an interesting exercise to watch the number of Liberal government spokesmen assume the role of critic, one usually reserved for our side of the House. We have had the more positive role of taking the government side. Let me assure hon. members opposite, Mr. Speaker, that this is a position my party and my leader readily accept.

I do not wish to dwell too long on this subject, but long enough to say that our proposed policy is one which offers tax recognition and relief to Canadians who have worked hard and saved to buy homes of their own. These are the forgotten people of the Canadian tax system who put up most of the money and make relatively little demand on many public services.
The Progressive Conservative party does not accept the Liberal no-growth scenario of the future. It means death to our communities. Our party is the only one to accept that growth must be an economic policy. Originally, the concept of government was that taxpayers would finance the administration to contribute to the economy. We now seem to be caught in the position of trying to administer the economy to finance the government. For 16 per cent of every Liberal government dollar goes to finance the national debt, which will reach $100 billion next year.

The government will have the dubious distinction of being known as the government of default by default. On behalf of the Conservative party, the future government, I make no apology for the fact that we recognize it is high time that Canadians were given some recognition and some incentive to keep up the hard work on which this country was built. That means we would not continue with a tax system which penalizes young couples who want a home and young children. Mr. Speaker, it means turning our tax system around to reward those who produce and those who save in order to provide the capital for the expansion of our economic base, which in turn provides the jobs for our chidren.
After the minister's trip to Toronto on Wednesday of last week, I thought it would be interesting to read the Globe and Mail. It said:
No, Mr. Ouellet's proposal falls down on its own demerits. Whatever its failings, Mr. Clark's mortgage deductibility program was aimed at reducing the high inventory of houses on the market, prompting a boom in the housing industry, and reactivating the economy. What Mr. Ouellet suggests is, quite simply, a redistribution of wealth, and the obvious question is, why is he cloaking a plan to cut taxes in something that resembles a housing policy?
The answer, we fear, is that the federal government, anxious to be seen as all things by all people, delights in creating special categories which appeal to special sectors of voters. Mothers get a cheque, families with low income get a cheque, everyone gets a cheque-less a policy than a determined effort to disguise a lack of policy. With any luck, the builders' reaction-one of disappointment-should convince Mr. Ouellet, and his government, to leave this particular kite on the conference floor.
This is one time I happen to really agree with the Globe and Mail.
February 26, 1979

One of the remaining elements in the bill emphasizes new expanded use of NHA mortgage insurance. In point of fact, the aggregate maximum of loan insurance has been increased to $40 billion and we hope to spend more time in committee in this area. The AHOP program has been dropped in favour of a graduated mortgage payment. Major lending institutions do not support this financing technique and to gain this support the government proposes to implement a quick settlement package. In the words of one analyst, "there are no longer any checks and balances; no rules for circumspection. The borrowers can borrow with hardly any money down. The lenders can lend with scant attention to risk. And CMHC can subsidize with magnanimous indifference."
I would like to read a little more, Mr. Speaker. I think it is important to quote, for instance, from the magazine "Finance". I refer to an item headed "The federal mortgage mess: will the banks help bail out Ottawa?" It is by Stephen Raikes:
It started out last winter as an election plum-yet another program to help thousands of "average Canadians" buy homes they would otherwise be hard pressed to afford.
Now, several months after the election-campaign-that-never-was, Ottawa's Graduated Payment Mortgage (GPM) program looks more like a badly shriveled prune-
Suppose for instance that a house buyer needs to borrow $35,000 at 10!4 per cent for 25 years... The unpleasant but less obvious fact is that over the life of the debt the GPM will cost the borrower $9,324 more than the standard mortgage would-$105,024 compared with $95,700. In those early years his payments aren't large enough even to cover all the interest, let alone retire any of the principal. As a result, he's obliged later on to pay interest on his unpaid interest. Thus his debt, rather than being retired, gradually increases-
Understandably, there are people in the world of finance who wonder whether there is a house buyer anywhere in Canada who really needs that kind of "help" from his federal government.
W. Peter Carter, past chairman of the mortgage committee of the Canadian Bankers' Association, has coined his own term for this. He calls it "GPM, the Permadebt." I think this is a very serious side to the graduated payment mortgage, Mr. Speaker, and we must take much more time to debate it. We must spend time in committee on its detail.
On the one hand we have the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) who wants to continue to wrestle inflation to the ground, and on the other we have the Minister of State for Urban Affairs phasing in graduated payment mortgages based on future inflationary increases in prices and incomes. We are putting people into a dreadful box if we pass this piece of legislation.
The Minister of Finance claimed some months ago that the money spent under the present government went to build houses and increase supply, not to create expectation and demand higher prices. In fact, scarcity of serviced lots and high carrying costs due to zoning delays combined with this government's own demand initiatives equal unprecedented housing inflation over the past four years. This problem is now compounded by the fact that residential construction activity is bound to decline if the current large inventory of newly constructed but unoccupied dwellings is not absorbed.
Housing
To compensate for this decline in residential building activity the minister has encouraged the home building industry to become actively involved in the new co-operative and non-profit form of housing. In a speech he made last Friday the minister went to great lengths to describe this. But what worries me is the statement the hon. gentleman made last September when he was discussing the CMHC budget cuts. The minister urged sponsors of low income housing projects to give up their preoccupation with the design and construction of new housing. He went on to say, and I quote:
I believe that low income housing sponsors would be wise to consider seriously the "best buy" principle and look toward existing housing for their clients rather than think in terms of new structures.
I hope the people in the private sector will recognize what the minister was saying here. I am warning them now that he will probably try to get rid of the 53,000 AHOP homes before he lets them go ahead.
Mr. Adamson of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation indicated last year in a speech in Windsor that while the new non-profit program promises to do a better job of bringing adequate accommodation within the reach of many people, it is not likely to have a massive effect on the production of new housing. I think this is one thing this House and this government must realize. While it is imperative that we encourage this side of our community life, we must realize that it represents only a very small proportion of what must be done in the housing market.
As for the termination of the old AHOP, the minister is certainly aware of my evaluation of that program. However, I believe it is important for us to examine for the record the actual success of this program because I believe it mirrors the future of the graduated mortgage payment as it is being proposed at the moment. The graduated mortgage payment is much worse, from the government's point of view, because there will be an automatic payout with any account three months in arrears.
I would like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that AHOP foreclosures increased by 463 per cent in 1978 over 1977. That is to say, the number of AHOP foreclosures increased from 265 to 1,492. AHOP foreclosures now account for 56 per cent of all mortgages acquired by the mortgage insurance fund. Furthermore, we have stated that the default rate approximates 10 per cent. In recent correspondence the minister indicated that it is 1.62 per cent of direct loans administered by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, up marginally, he said, from the 1.31 per cent of a year ago. However, a year ago in the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs he indicated that the default rate was 5.6 per cent, up from 5.1 per cent, and records show that by March of 1978 the rate was 8 per cent.
Now the minister states that there are 36,000 AHOP accounts under administration. One year ago there were 39,000. Changing the definition does not remove the fact that there are hundreds, if not thousands, of AHOP purchasers
3586

February 26, 1979
Housing
who are now having difficulties in meeting their shelter expenditures. It is a common joke within the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that the minister is operating the best key club in Ontario because people just mail in their keys.
Meetings called "disaster meetings" are held at the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation with regard to AHOP foreclosures, but the minister will not even answer our questions about them in this House. What is even more alarming is the growing number of reports daily about lack of quality construction in many AHOP homes, in violation of the national building code. I am aware that in the spirit of good politics a man should mend his fences. If this holds true for this program, the minister had better start "fixin". The question this raises is, what does it actually mean when a project is advertised as "government approved" or "CMHC approved"? According to the minister or his ex-parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), the slogan or advertisement "CMHC approved" means nothing. Indeed, according to the ex-parliamentary secretary, the government could not care less what happens to the houses. The only inspection which is supposed to be carried out pertains to the advancement of mortgage money. We know from the growing number of reports and the increase in the number of active RCMP investigations that the government cannot even manage this. This is one of the hidden tragedies.
How many people have driven by these projects and seen the label of the Government of Canada on them, and how many have thought that they were buying a good product? This is a serious matter which must be investigated and rectified.
I found it particularly enlightening to review another confidential study of the department which reads in part as follows:
Provision of insurance entails appraisal and inspection of units and this served to provide a kind of guarantee to purchasers on the quality and workmanship of their unit.
The question, of course, is whether or not we can describe the kind of guarantee which is referred to in that cabinet document.
Before I leave completely the housing mortgage issue, I think I should make it clear that if the minister had anything to say last week in Toronto, one thing was clear: housing is not a priority of this government at this time. We on this side feel that housing is a basic right of every Canadian, and to us it is priority.
If the so-called Canadian housing crisis means anything, the lack of affordable and meaningful choice is its characteristic. Many Canadians have been forced into the no housing choice position in which a third to one half of their regular income goes for shelter. In this process they do not necessarily gain better quality but may be forced into accommodation which is considered by any set of criteria to be substandard. The changing pattern of ownership and tenancy is a response to what is available, not an exercise of choice.
To many Canadians this lack of choice means that the user requirements are not being met. User requirements have physical, social and environmental aspects. Physical requirements relate to a concern about the individual house and its heating,

plumbing and wiring systems. They pertain to structural safety and to the development and determination of housing standards which will engender good public health. At least half the total housing stock in the 1970s was created prior to 1945, and a fair proportion of it was built in the first quarter of the century or earlier. This very substantial amount of reasonably good old housing deserves our profound attention during the balance of this century. This party feels very strongly that this is a priority.
User requirements, however, should be seen in a much wider context. A dwelling is located in a neighbourhood, and much more attention should be paid to the wider environment as one of the important aspects of user concern. Therefore, user requirements must be conceived as social and environmental in nature rather than merely physical.
One of the toughest tasks for business today is to foresee what tomorrow's customers will want to buy. The industry with the bleakest outlook is housing, and that has ominous implications for the rest of the economy. That is why mortgage interest deductibility and property tax deduction proposals are part of our policy. We care about the economy as well as about housing.
Earl Bederman, assistant vice president and economist for the Permanent Trust Company, has said:
The future for housing isn't what it used to be. The annual population growth from now until the end of the century will be 1 per cent compared with 3 per cent of the 1950s. Actual requirements for new housing will take a dive in the mid-1980s.
Bederman estimates that by the end of the century requirements will be 40 per cent lower than they are today. Over the long run, and I quote again:
Real estates markets are likely to get more fragile.
As house prices decline, home owners could find themselves with high mortgages but lower equity. We are getting very close to the point where equity-carrying cost ratios will tilt in favour of more walk-away situations and outright defaults. Price declines in the order of 25 per cent to 30 per cent cannot be ruled out. That is why we have to have a review of AHOP, and we must look very carefully at graduated mortgage payments.
What opportunities there will be in construction should be in smaller-sized homes, duplexes and row housing. The renovation business will boom. It already accounts for 35 per cent of the residential construction market, and analysts feel that it will continue to be the fastest growing sector over the next few years. This must be encouraged by the federal government.
Experimentation in the social and environmental aspects of user requirements should be actively encouraged. Experimentation is required at four levels: the street, the immediate neighbourhood, the subregions within an urban area and the broader community. In short, we must have emphasis on experimentation. Funds must be made available which make much more possible active experimentation in new ways of building our communities. To this end, government and businesses must provide the funds necessary for experimentation to adapt our communities to new forms of living in the remaining
February 26, 1979

part of this century. We must find incentives for the unorthodox builder. The "thou shalt not" philosophy should be replaced by a policy of encouraging social and physical innovation. The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the provincial housing corporations are in a strategic position to provide leadership in such an effort.
The great tragedy is the wasted years of this ministry. I find it strange to read again the comments which the minister made last Friday. Never once did he mention what was going to happen to the people, the policies and the projects that had been started in the ministry. Who is going to care for this in the federal government when the ministry is phased out on April 1? What will happen to CMHC? It is one of the saddest things to have to stand here today and comment about that wonderful organization of the past called CMHC. The minister seems to want to change its name, and I wonder why.
In the question period I asked for an investigation into CMHC by the Auditor General because I believe we must clean up a sad and desperate situation out there. It is rather hard to read into the record what has happened to CMHC under the direction of the minister. I could talk about York Place, luxury hotels, Cloverdale, I could mention Virginia Park, the great home insulation program that never got off the ground, that great tragedy called Walter Rudnicki, the $15,000 staff tournaments, Quigley Road, and land banking. 1 could read into the record the series of five articles in which the Hamilton Spectator wrote about such things as $500,000 for 12 basements, the RCMP probe into housing disasters, 150 Sanford, how the developers' pie was sweetened. But what I need to read really is the very fine editorial which appeared in the Spectator of February 3 entitled "Time to Evaluate CMHC". It reads:
When short-term political considerations become more important than good planning and competent management, taxpayers can expect to find themselves footing the bills without receiving any benefits.
In a probing series of articles published last week, Spectator reporter. John Kernaghan revealed how the corporation has been used as a political tool for several years now. As a result, CMHC may have wasted millions of taxpayers' dollars over the last ten years.
If CMHC had stuck to its original purpose and remained a lending institution, chances are it would be a respected and substantial part of today's housing industry. However, government pressures for social involvement and the consequent use of CMHC as a way to influence voters through such programs as low income housing projects, native housing projects and modified handouts such as the Assisted Home Ownership Plan have left the Crown corporation with some major, and unnecessary, financial white elephants on its hands.
CMHC's current problems apparently stem from a combination of political pressure coupled with a lack of ministerial responsibility and an absence of accountability ... On the other hand, there is also considerable evidence that the federal government frequently ignored the recommendations of CMHC inspectors and officials.
We have terrible tragedies which should be investigated, Mr. Speaker. There is one called 150 Sanford. I believe that there should be an immediate investigation into this area. The editorial goes on to read:
As a first step in cleaning up CMHC's problems, the minister responsible for the agency must exert control over the corporation's plans and its budget-
Housing
Finally, CMHC should not be used as yet another job creation agency or as a vehicle for social form. Its original purpose was to provide funds to home owners, not to developers, and it should return to its role as a funding agency.
To a great extent, the problem stems from the present government's lack of coherent planning and its tendency to distort valid programs to political ends. The unemployment insurance scheme and CMHC are prime examples of the messes that can result.
Since Canada now has a declining birth rate and a temporary housing surplus, it is an ideal time to have the Auditor General review the management policies of CMHC and determine how well taxpayers' money is being spent.

To come back to my comments, sir, may I point out that policymakers must come to recognize that we have a considerable technical knowledge of house building, of the servicing of land and of the provision of physical facilities within a house, on a street or in a neighbourhood, but that we have very little knowledge about meeting people's social and community needs. A major objective is to obtain that knowledge.
This is not to say that we should attempt to obtain this understanding in isolation. Whatever experimentation is going to be tried should be intimately embraced within the systems approach. It should be part of the effort to obtain a better understanding of the urban system. Already many innovations have been made in Canadian urban life. What has often been lacking is the monitoring of these innovations. It is only through organized and systematic monitoring of experiments that answers can be obtained on what works and does not. Probably the major concern that needs to be addressed in housing today is the affordability problem and the promise of industrialization within the housing industry. It is to their credit that the industry has been able to produce as well as it has within the constraints that have developed around it and within it.
However, increased attention must be given to the regional variations in housing construction. As well, qualitative criteria for human habitations must be incorporated. It can no longer remain a policy of guaranteeing mortgage risk only to have the house deteriorate some months after the work is finished. The national building code should not be a static document. Input must come from architects, scientists, psychologists and many others in the formulation of a realistic code that will reflect regional quantitative and qualitative standards for housing.
Other constraints include financing, training and land assembly. I should make reference to the land component. Although a recent study, the Greenspan report, indicated that it was a mistake for government to have initiated land assembly programs when they did, the fact is that affordability and choice could be bettered if policies were launched which utilized the public funded land banks now in existence. We must address ourselves to land banks. We have close to $1

Returning to the area of land banking, in the long run the forms and procedures for those measures of public ownership which might be required must be the object of study and consultation among the three levels of government. As a parliamentarian, I realize there is an urgent necessity to find a new role for government, sensitive to the complexities of contemporary urban problems.
In the interest of freeing the creative potential of government, I am suggesting a major retreat from processes of heavy bureaucratic supervision of urban programs involving two or more levels of government. Governments as providers of public services must recognize that passing papers of approvals and counterapprovals is a costly, soul-destroying process which can grind the system to a halt. Changing the style of governing will
(Mrs. Pigott.]
take a new sense of maturity, but trade-offs in the way of greater productivity and rationalization of roles should more than offset the imagined losses of control.
One by-product of the new style would be the releasing of provincial and federal governments to concentrate on public policy issues appropriate to their place in the total government system. In urban policy these would be issues related to broad development patterns, the structure of population, employment and services, and the structure of underlying financial allocations and industrial strategies which reverberate on the entire urban system. These sentiments are echoed in a book entitled: "Changing Canadian Cities-The Next 25 Years" by Len Gertler and Ron Crowley. This book contains one of the best quotations concerning urban policy which I have read in a long time. In part it reads as follows:
Looking at the evolution of policy and government I cannot resist the observation that Canadian urban policies are unfulfilled. As a nation in search of a formula to stay united, we are still attempting to carry over into this age of uncertainty the attitudes and styles of government from long ago. The adjustment we make to the demands of our time may determine whether the chroniclers of 2000 A.D. will characterize our period as the "age of wisdom and mature democracy" or of "mismanagement and misguided authority".
The government has failed in controlling inflation, in creating employment for hundreds of young people, and has also missed one of the greatest opportunities of this decade. By concentrating on housing starts the government missed laying the groundwork and planning for Canadian urban living in the 1980s and 1990s. It did not concentrate on affordability and quality of shelter. It did not listen to the grassroots of the nation, the people who want to create community living which will make urban centres liveable and maintain the fundamental social building blocks which make up our society: the family unit, school, church, the work place and the municipal hall. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) told us in his speech last Friday that Canadians are among the best housed people in the world, that there is no housing crisis in

Canada, that we have an acceptable level of housing production and that the cost of housing is within the financial capacity of those who live in homes. It was such a pleasant and complacent picture that some of us, I am sure, were wondering why we have any housing programs at all and, indeed, whether any are needed.
There is a great deal of distance between the minister's picture of Canadian housing and the experience of the poor people in Winnipeg and elsewhere. Just two years ago the then chairman of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, Mr. Teron, made a speech in Calgary in November 1976, and he was quoted as saying:
When 280,000 families in Canada pay more than 50 per cent of their family income for housing, 550,000 families in Canada pay more than 45 per cent, 820,000 families pay more than 25 per cent, and two-thirds of Canadians in need of housing cannot afford to buy or rent without a subsidy from their fellow man, we have a fundamental problem-we must take reasonable action now, or more drastic action later.
Has the situation changed in just over two years from the time Mr. Teron made that speech? Just over a few weeks ago there was a special report on housing which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune which said among other things:
Several thousand Winnipeg families, including about 3,000 headed by single women, face a bleak winter in housing conditions described as "poor," "substandard" and "dumpy," while three levels of government back away from the low-income housing problem.
Recently, there was a strange situation in my city where the city council, composed mostly of Conservatives, refused to go ahead with a $1 million low-income housing project, despite the fact that in so doing they were rejecting substantial amounts of money offered by the federal government and the provincial government. The federal response to the reality of low income policy was nicely summarized by a CMHC regional economist in Winnipeg, Mr. Karl Falk, who said:
Our official party line is that housing is a provincial matter, we are only in there by default.
No provincial government has the financial resources to singlehandedly tackle the housing problem, but we in Manitoba must deal with a Tory provincial government which has not authorized any new family public housing since it took office. They want to see if there is a need, according to the chairman of the provincial housing corporation, before they go ahead.
One group which the minister did not listen to while deciding that Canada has no housing problem is the Institute for Urban Affairs in Winnipeg which, incidentally, is headed by a very prominent Fiberal, Mr. Floyd Axworthy, the man who they would like to see as a Fiberal candidate in the next federal election and who spent several years in Ottawa as special assistant to the then minister of housing, Mr. Hellyer. The institute's assistant director said in the same issue of the Tribune:
It leaves me very disturbed because someone has to take responsibility for making sure housing needs are met. No one seems willing to play that role, and the private sector is not going to pick up the slack.
That is what that institute thinks of the federal government's so-called housing policy.
February 26, 1979

There is a great deal of slack in the Winnipeg housing situation which could be taken up. A recent report found that my city has both a large stock of older, poor quality, deteriorating housing in the inner city and an inner city community which is deteriorating in strength and vitality. Thirty-seven per cent of Winnipeg renters pay more than one quarter of their income on rent, a situation which is worse only in Vancouver among the major Canadian cities. People in Winnipeg see nothing in the housing situation about which they can be complacent, despite what the minister said last Friday.
What will be the effect of this bill when it is enacted? This bill will implement the changes which were included in the amendments to the National Housing Act last May under the title "New Directions in Housing." This statement called for a number of things, among which were included:
-an end to the generous aid to co-ops and non-profits started during the minority parliament and its replacement by less expensive subsidies.
-an end to rent supplements (50-50 federal-provincial) for co-op, non-profit, provincial or municipal housing units.
-an end to loans to provinces or municipalities for the construction of public housing and to the 50-50 sharing of operating losses in such projects; CMHC will continue to offer provinces a partnership arrangement in public housing (federal government pays 75 per cent of capital cost and operating losses).
The provinces do not care much for this option as it involves too much interference by Central Mortgage and Housing. One of the goals of the new directions was supposedly to end this type of interference.
There is also an end to the assisted home ownership program and an end to the assisted rental program-both of which received such glowing comments when they were proposed by this government-and the introduction of the graduated payment mortgage which was insured but not offered by CMHC. Like AHOP, it simply postpones the monthly mortgage payment you cannot afford now to a later date when your situation will be even worse.
There was also the expansion of the types of mortgages which CMHC can insure to make up for the fact CMHC no longer lends money. There was an expansion of the residential rehabilitation program, but without the funds to implement it. There was an end to the municipal infrastructure program for water and sewer construction, the municipal incentive program which provided grants for medium density housing, and the neighbourhood improvement program and its replacement by the community services program which provides less money for a wider range of projects.
I should like to quote again from the article in the Winnipeg Tribune of January 31, 1979, on the effect of just one of the proposals. Referring to the non-profit housing program, the article reads as follows:
Under the old program, CMHC provided low interest loans for such non-profit housing corporations as the provincial government's MHRC and native people's KINEW. While it attached the string of rents held to 25 per cent of tenants' incomes (where rental housing was involved), it made that string elastic through rent supplements. Under the new program, financing must be obtained through the private sector-
Housing
The private sector does not want this burden.
-although the federal government will provide generous interest reduction grants. But to qualify for the grants, the non-profit corporations must meet the 25 per cent rental requirements without the elastic feature of rent supplements. Section 44-IB of the National Housing Act, which provided for rent supplements to fill the gap between the cost of housing and the 25 per cent of income standard of affordability, has been discontinued.
Stan Fulham, head of KINEW-
KINEW is a native housing organization which has done a very fine job of providing housing for native people in Winnipeg.
-the non-profit corporation geared to provide housing to native people, figures the program won't be much help for low income families. "Even with a two per cent interest rate, you're still taking $200 or more a month. So for the low income people, it's no help. KINEW's going to be forced to discriminate. If there's no subsidy available to them, they just won't be able to afford our housing. They'll have to take substandard slum housing."
That is what one of the most active groups which provides housing for people in Winnipeg who cannot afford housing in the conventional way has to say about the government's proposals.
I want to look now at the community services program which groups together all the old programs such as non-profit housing, co-operative housing, sewer and water extention, the neighbourhood improvement program and so on. The government says it is willing to adopt a global approach to its financial aid to municipalities, and to achieve this it proposes to take ten individual programs, each of which requires well in excess of $25 million for Canada as a whole, and lump them together to produce what it calls a new global approach, for a maximum of $250 million per year instead of the $339 million which was allocated for all these programs last year. That is an economic sleight-of-hand. The government expects the provinces and the municipalities to thank them for this.
The federal government has indicated that it wants to produce flexibility and wider latitude for the provinces and municipalities in using federal funds, to enable federal assistance to better respond to local needs and conditions, to reduce duplication and to ensure that assistance is available equally to all provinces.
We must look beyond the kind of rhetoric the minister used last Friday. As we have seen many times before with this government, rhetoric and action are clearly two different things. To the extent that this program is obviously long on rhetoric, it is correspondingly short on action. It is particularly short on funding, Mr. Speaker, which, as I have already indicated, has been cut back very substantially this year because of the government's restraint program. It uses expressions like "great" and "ongoing", but what do they mean? In 1973, after an irresponsible delay of five critical years during which urban renewal programs were cut off, the new NIP program was brought forth. In 1978, almost before most municipalities learned to make effective use of the neighbourhood improvement program, the government took it away, merging it with such a variety of other demanding programs that it will be, in effect, emasculated.

February 26, 1979
Housing
A close look at the neighbourhood improvement program and its operation shows exactly how it was emasculated. Under the old legislation, if an area was designated for improvement under NIP it was automatically eligible for the residential rehabilitation assistance program. Now under the community services program there is no guarantee that RRAP funding will be available to people in the neighbourhood improvement area. The neighbourhood improvement program will fail without those rehabilitation funds. That failure will be felt by the residents of neighbourhoods in the Winnipeg area such as the Chalmers area in Elmwood and the Daniel McIntyre area in west Winnipeg. These areas had hoped to be able to benefit from the program which since 1973 have made a great difference in other Winnipeg neighbourhoods which have benefited from the start of them.
The necessity of keeping the automatic link with the neighbourhood improvement program and the residential rehabilitation assistance program was illustrated in the Point Douglas project, a Winnipeg neighbourhood which had become quite run down. There are between 650 and 700 dwellings in that area. They received 480 RRAP loans with the result that it is now a much better neighbourhood for people to live in and to raise their families. The same thing can be seen in other neighbourhood improvement programs around Winnipeg. Point Douglas received RRAP grants for 70 per cent of the homes. There was also RRAP funding for 280 homes in the Centennial area, representing between 50 per cent and 60 per cent of homes in that area. In St. Boniface 40 per cent of homes under the NIP program received RRAP funds. It is estimated that under another NIP program in the William Whyte area about 80 per cent of the homes will need RRAP money for rehabilitation. This is at a time when the government has decided to cut back on the amount of RRAP funding and make it more difficult to obtain.
There has been a direct relationship between the use of funds to improve a neighbourhood and funds to rehabilitate the housing in that neighbourhood. However, community services grants for those two purposes will not be automatically linked. They will just be part of the many deserving programs that must suddenly make do with a much smaller global budget. This is going to deny the chance of real improvement to many neighbourhoods in Winnipeg. What is true in Winnipeg is true in other cities across Canada. The government does not care. Instead of worrying about these neighbourhoods it is involved in a game it has been playing for years-offer the neighbourhoods, the communities and cities of Canada lots of sizzle and when they try to taste the steak, pull it away.
For the past ten years, in fact for the past 35 to 40 years, extensive areas of housing and urban development have been built in this country without adequate storm sewers, community facilities, solid waste disposal, urban transport and many other essential services. For the past three years, for example, AHOP has been touted as a great solution for moderate income housing. But housing in what kind of urban environment? In my own area the best municipal officials can suggest, to prevent a brand new AHOP and NHA financed housing
[Mr. Orlikow.l
project from having basements flooded with raw sewage five or six times a year, is to fill a nearby artifical lake built for storm water retention and to divert raw sewage into it. What a commentary on the kind of planning this government has done in recent years!
This housing was built by developers who are well known supporters of the Liberal party. It got CMHC approval and encouragement to build on lands which were totally inadequate with respect to storm and sanitary sewage facilities.
With problems like this burgeoning in urban developments across the country, even if $100 million out of the proposed $250 million was used to correct problems such as those which have been created in my constituency, it would be barely enough to finance a fraction of what needs to be done to correct damage resulting from poorly administered NHA programs.
In other words, the Liberal government in Ottawa wants to bail out and leave the province and municipalities with inadequate funding to clean up the mess left by its ill-conceived programs. Furthermore, in the mad rush to get starts in place, no precautions were taken. Its funding arrangements are not even equitable in terms of the population of the regions of the country. In Manitoba's case, instead of receiving $12'/2 million it has been offered only $10 million.
Before getting away from this subject, I want to warn the minister that as a result of a decision handed down last week by the Supreme Court of Canada which held that a municipality which had drained part of a suburb of Ottawa without taking adequate precautions so that homes already built had substantial damage done to their foundations was responsible for this situation and would probably have to pay damages. I hope that the residents of my area will go after the city and the developers who were so negligent that they built over 1,000 houses without providing for the run-off of rain water, which resulted in houses being flooded, although they should have known and I think did know that they were not providing adequate storm sewers for the area.
What about Canadians who presumably manage to purchase their own homes? Despite what the minister said, Canadians are house poor. The high cost of housing is absorbing a large portion of an individual's total income every year. We had better start looking carefully at our assumptions concerning housing and land. Since 1945 the single family dwelling located on a large lot has become the ideal form of housing which most Canadians aspired to. In the 1950s it was possible for the average Canadian to own his own home. A generation later his sons and daughters cannot do the same thing.
Each week I receive a list of new homes purchased in the city of Winnipeg. I look particularly at the ones purchased in my own constituency. From this list I can see people who are buying homes at prices of $60,000, $70,000, $80,000 and $90,000, and I wonder how they will manage to make the mortgage payments on those homes. They have committed
February 26, 1979

themselves for the next 25 years to monthly payments that run anywhere from $300 to $600 a month. This is a burden which many of them will find impossible to carry in the next few years.
In spite of the increase in family income since 1961, the ability of people to afford a house in those cities has actually decreased. A study done in Winnipeg comparing 1961 and 1975 prices found that family incomes had increased by 100 per cent in that time, but the price of a new house in the suburbs had increased by 152 per cent. And if you add to that the increase in monthly payments which reflects both higher housing prices and higher mortgage interest rates, the increase was 219 per cent.
Right now the average price of a house in metropolitan Toronto is $68,500 and it is anticipated that the price will rise another 7 per cent to 8 per cent over the next year. In the central core it is even higher; the average there is $80,000. With mortgage rates now at a high of 11.25 per cent, the dream has become almost unattainable. Just who is buying houses?
In the few Canadians cities where suburban lots are still reasonably priced, moderate income families can still afford suburban single family houses. In 1976 in Halifax 66 per cent of all new house buyers under NHA had incomes of less than $15,000. In Saskatoon 56 per cent of all new house buyers had incomes less that $15,000. Those were two cities where some lots were controlled by municipal government. But in cities with high land prices the figures are very different. In Toronto only 7 per cent of new house buyers had incomes less than $15,000. In Winnipeg it was 8 per cent and in Edmonton only 4 per cent.
It would appear that moderate and low income families are unable to afford the great Canadian dream of owning their own homes. The housing market presently caters to the middle and upper class. Today's typical family needs an annual income of nearly $30,000 to buy a new home in metropolitan Toronto. One of the reasons for the very substantial increase in the cost of a home in Canada has to do with the cost of land. That is something we should be looking at very carefully. The cost of raw land has increased, but in the total cost of lots it is a relatively modest factor.
It has been the practice of many developers to assemble private land banks in anticipation of future needs. What one CMHC researcher discovered is that a small number of developers hold enough land to supply all new suburban lots which will be required for the next five to 15 years. And because they control the land assemblies, a few developers are able to control the market in ways that lead the price increases for suburban house lots. Between 1971 and 1976 house prices have doubled in most cities. The price increases are not from higher costs of production, but rather from increases in profits developers have made on the land. A recent study has documented that profits by the large suburban land developers added $7,000 to $10,000 to the price of new $50,000 homes in Regina and Winnipeg. In cities like Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto and Ottawa profits added $15,000 to $24,000 to the
Housing
price of a $60,000 home. Just west of Toronto the Peel housing task force found that profits on lots were 22 per cent of the final selling price of the house.
It is large land owners making windfall profits on the sale of their property who are escalating the cost of housing. Land, urban land in particular, we believe should be treated as a scarce resource in much the same way as other natural resources. Under the present system we are allowing a few people to effectively control the supply and cost of land. But it is not only the cost of housing that they control; they also dictate the options as to the kind of housing available. It is either housing everyone wants but few can afford, or housing that everyone can afford but few want.
If hon. members doubt my charge that the developers are making exorbitant profits, let me quote from an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune dated October 31, 1978. This article was written by Val Werier who writes a column almost every day in that newspaper. It reads:
In northwest Winnipeg-
This is an area within my constituency.
-a market gardener sold his 32 acres in 1973 for $64,000, or $2,000 an acre. In 1977, the new owners were listing it at $500,000. This year they are asking $688,000 or about $21,000 an acre.
That is quite an increase in just six years. The article goes on to say:
Within the past five years, the asking price for some land in the northwest corner of the city has risen tenfold, according to one real estate agent.
"The speculators are taking homebuyers for a ride because of the high price for land," he says.
The real estate agent notes, for example, that eight acres were sold in 1975 for $72,500 near the site of the Seven Oaks hospital, now under construction. Today, the asking price for this raw land is about $400,000 because the new owner can capitalize on the huge public expenditures in the form of a hospital. The hospital will attract new developments such as apartment blocks.
That is the situation which we now face. The survey of housing units has provided new and up-to-date data that permit a better identification of the number of households suffering from some form of housing need, either dwelling unit inadequacy, overcrowding or problems of affordability. Overall about 60 per cent of all households in urban Canada had none of the above problems in 1974. About one third, or 1,025,000 households, have one problem only. Another 7 per cent encountered two or more problems and therefore had serious shelter inadequacies.
Of the approximately one third of 1,025,000 households that were suffering from some form of housing deprivation, 180,000 were living in inadequate dwellings, 298,000 were overcrowded and 547,000 were paying more than 25 per cent of total household income on shelter. Affordability therefore emerges as the largest single housing problem. Yet, Mr. Speaker, in his speech the minister did not pay any attention to the question of affordability. Listening to the minister, one would assume that he believes no one in Canada has any problem with affordability.

What we need to do, in our view, is provide funds for the projects covered by the community services program, and the $250 million proposed is not adequate. Second, we believe we should provide for co-operative, non-profit public housing. That money is not included in the estimates we have for next year. We believe the government should bring back its land assembly program.

We need to stop the rip-off which has taken place over the last number of years by developers who have made, are making and will make tremendous and exorbitant profits unless governments at three levels step in to carry out this land assembly program.
In addition, we need to provide adequate funds for the residential rehabilitation assistance program, and the estimates for next year do not provide for that. We need to force the banks to set mortgage rates at 8 per cent for families with incomes of $20,000 or less who want to buy homes that cost less than $50,000.
Those are the minimum steps we believe are necessary if we are to meet the housing needs of the people of Canada. We certainly do not see those steps in this bill and we do not see the funds provided for in the estimates we have before us for the coming year. We did not hear about these things in the speech of the minister last Friday. For those reasons we certainly intend to vote against this bill.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure and an honour to participate in this debate. I should like to support these amendments to the National Housing Act for a number of reasons. During the debate so far we have heard a considerable amount of discussion in respect of the mortgage deductibility program proposed by members of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. Recently, as the House knows, an all party committee went to Washington to examine with U.S. representatives and other officials the issue of mortgage deductibility. The all party committee was comprised of the hon. members for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke), Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott), Broadview (Mr. Rae), Westmount (Mr. Johnston) and Stormont-Dundas (Mr. Lumley). In a memorandum prepared by the hon. member for Westmount, he concluded:
A recommendation of all government officials and all independent economists with whom we met was to the effect that a system of mortgage interest or real estate tax deductibility is to be avoided at all costs.
The hon. member for Westmount went on to say:
Because the proposed deductions favour high income owners the measure is regressive, and in lieu of promoting tax neutrality it offends the principle, because it discriminates against tenants and non-homeowners. Because it selects only real estate taxes for deduction there would be a shift of local taxation into the real estate tax area with less emphasis being placed in other areas of local taxation.
Because of the regressive nature of this provision the benefits derived would tend to favour owners of existing homes, providing them with more disposable incomes while doing much less for income groups anxious to enter the housing market, and doing nothing for those at the low end of the income scale without sufficient income to take advantage of these deductions. The effect of this would
Adjournment Motion
be to widen the economic gap between the rich and the poor, between home owners and non-home owners.
Adequate studies have not been performed to determine what impact the deductibility of mortgage interest and real estate taxes would have on urban communities. For example, to what extent would the centre core properties be purchased and renovated as the result of this scheme, driving tenants and owners in these low income areas into substandard housing and substandard accommodation? What impact would this particular mortgage deductibility scheme have on the urban sprawl and on the pressure for condominiumization of apartments, with the resulting impact on our tenant population?
In brief, no fiscal program which would alter the basic structure of the tax system should be introduced without the most thorough study and analysis of the kind now being carried on by the Urban Institute for HUD in the United States. Once in place it cannot be easily modified and its social consequences can be farreaching.
Because of its regressive nature I reject the proposal of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. Instead, I firmly believe that a tax credit system would be more beneficial as it assists low income earners regardless of whether they are home owners or renters. Also the use of tax shelters would help people like senior citizens who need more direct assistance because they are not able to have the advantage of progressive incomes.
In short, I agree wholeheartedly that shelter tax allowances will provide assistance to home owners and tenants alike through payment of a tax credit shelter expenditure exceeding a certain percentage of income in the right way. As I indicated, I support these amendments to the National Housing Act for a number of reasons. They represent a reasonable approach to housing problems across a very broad front.
I am particularly pleased that the bill preserves and extends one of the most important housing measures ever put forward here in Canada. I am referring to the residential rehabilitation assistance program, otherwise known as RRAP. I am delighted to see that the government has removed or intends to remove the restrictions from this program, that its benefits are no longer going to be restricted to certain designated areas but will apply to Canadians wherever they live. With the passage of this legislation all Canadians will become eligible for RRAP assistance within the terms of the program, and I have no doubt that the funds available to support it will be applied to more pressing needs wherever they occur in Canada.
I am not surprised that RRAP met with such immediate enthusiastic response by the people of Canada. RRAP and its twin, neighbourhood improvement, actually originated in the Strathcona area located in my riding.
If it is the pleasure of the House, may I call it five o'clock?
