subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF INSTITUTING INDIVIDUAL INCOME STABILIZATION PROGRAM FOR WESTERN PRODUCERS
speechtext:
That the Standing Committee on Agriculture be empowered to study the advisability of instituting an individual rather than aggregate program of income stabilization for the western producer, and to report its findings to the House.
He said: Mr. Speaker, over the years I have given much thought to stabilization as a means of helping farmers in all of Canada but particularly in western Canada, and as an attempt to eliminate the so-called hills and valleys in the production of commodities and in the prices producers get for those commodities. We have examined various plans in order to accomplish this. Producers have attempted to accomplish it by means of supply management marketing boards. Various government stabilization plans have been instituted and a number of income tax techniques are available to farmers, but it is my belief that members of parliament and the Standing Committee on Agriculture as a whole should take a very serious look at individual stabilization as the plan of the future in order to help farmers adequately stabilize their incomes.
Since I arrived here as a member in 1972 I have considered it a pleasure to serve on the Standing Committee on Agriculture because I have felt it has always done an excellent job of dealing with questions put before it. I remember that when it was dealing with the Western Grain Stabilization Act the committee travelled to western Canada to learn the opinions of western farmers as to whether we should have that legislation and, if we should, whether amendments or changes should be
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
made to it. I found at that time that a number of members were questioning whether we should have aggregate stabilization, that is, stabilization of the whole area, or individual stabilization of some sort which might be better suited to regions or to particular problems.
While the committee was on that trip, this question was asked many times, and I have here a few responses from witnesses who came before that committee. One response came from the hon. John Messer, then minister of agriculture of the province of Saskatchewan. He said:
The plan does not provide individual commodity or regional income stability. No account is taken for regional, geographic and climatic factors which influence the production of various grains throughout the prairies.
When we were in Manitoba the hon. Sam Uskiw, the then Manitoba minister of agriculture, said:
It seems to me that since the proposed grain stabilization act is being portrayed as an income insurance scheme and since it is a contributory plan, farmers should know what insurance they are buying; in other words, the plan must relate to the needs of individuals, and it should be possible for individuals to determine what benefits would accrue to them if the events against which they are insuring themselves should occur.
Many members of the committee felt that the plan should be individual and perhaps administered by the crop insurance plan, which is active all across the prairies and has offices throughout the regions and people who are constantly travelling among farms. Here is a natural set-up by which an individual plan could be established. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) came up with a plan, and during a good part of the time he had in the committee he discussed whether an individual plan could be set up which could be administered by the crop insurance people. I also felt that there should be an individual plan, and I remember asking the then minister of agriculture of the province of Manitoba what his thoughts were. He stated them as follows:
If it was possible to base stabilization on the individual, that would mean that the province would have to administer it and I suspect the best way to administer it would be through crop insurance machinery that is already set up.
I do not necessarily agree that the plan would have to be administered by the province, but the then minister did state that he felt that the crop insurance people could administer such a plan.
The Palliser Wheat Growers Association stated the following:
If individual stabilization is the objective, the plan would be more effective if dovetailed with existing crop insurance programs.
I now come to the point where I must state that I fully believe that the individual stabilization method is the ultimate program for Canada, and I fully believe that if the Standing Committee on Agriculture were to study such a method, the majority of members of that committee would come to have the same opinion.
I would have no objection if we were to broaden my motion so that we could study a stabilization plan which would guarantee margins. I know that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has been discussing this with the provinces. Rather than having a 90 per cent level, the minister has been discussing perhaps a 100 per cent level plus cost of production
February 26, 1979

and other changes. However, I think members of parliament should get involved in such a study because farmers face rapidly rising production costs, to the extent that tractors and other machinery now cost two to three times more than they did only five years ago.
Because we are an exporting nation, world production fluctuations have a great influence on what the Canadian farmer earns. We have to give farmers a reasonable return on their investment or they will continue to leave agriculture and flock to the cities. That is why I introduced this private member's motion today. I am asking hon. members to give the Standing Committee on Agriculture the power to study the principle of stabilization on an individual basis. By doing so, hon. members might become informed about the benefits of such a plan. We must take this opportunity to achieve improved farm income stability at the farmer level.
Hon. members might say that there are a number of programs in place at the present time to do just that, and I agree that there is some truth in that. The first ones which come to mind are the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act. Those are both aggregate plans, and they cannot take account of regional and climatic factors and decisions of individual farmers as to what crops they plant, weed control, whether they stay in hogs or increase production of cattle. They do not take account of crop markets or price, which is often determined by world factors.
Of course, there is always government interference in the agricultural sector, and an aggregate plan cannot take account of that. Those plans are slow to pay. That was demonstrated by the first pay-out under the western grain stabilization plan. It took the government a year to make its first full payment. Half of it came six months after it should have come, and the other half came a full six months after that. There is a very complicated trigger formula which must be followed before payouts can be made, and there is also some room for the minister to decide when it is most politically advantageous.
There is another factor, and that is that one commodity can have an enormous effect on whether the trigger mechanism comes into play. Under the western grain stabilization plan wheat in the province of Saskatchewan bears too heavily on the trigger mechanism, and under the Agricultural Stabilization Act regional factors are not taken into consideration. Beef prices in Toronto are always five cents to seven cents higher than they are in western Canada, and because of that the averaging mechanism does not reflect the average price of beef in western Canada. So I find that these aggregate plans do not take into account the needs of the individual farmers. When a pay out occurs it benefits them, but in many cases when the need is there the stabilization plan is not.
Then there are such techniques as block averaging and general averaging, but the benefits of both tend to be in the years when farm incomes are the highest and the farmers do
Farm Income Stabilization
not really need them. We have deferred cash purchase tickets which are only available to grain farmers and also are used in high income years. Some farmers can use year-end purchasing as a stabilization factor. If they have a good year, they can buy their tractors before the end of the year. We can also have deferred sales. In effect, this is an individual plan because the farmer does not have to sell his grain; he can keep it in his bins and sell it the following year. But that does not help the Canadian economy because we must bring in foreign capital by selling our agricultural produce.
Then there is capital cost allowance, which is really depreciation and has been used for a number of years to help in income control.
All these programs are available, but true stabilization for a farmer on an individual basis does not exist today.
Some farmers are now attempting to use RRSPs for their own individual stabilization, but because withdrawals are limited-you cannot make partial withdrawals under this plan-farmers have to incur the cost of setting up many plans so that when they need money, they can draw from one of the plans and still have some money available for other years. This is complex but it shows that it is really what these farmers want. They are using what laws are available now to do just that.
I have come to the conclusion that none of these plans offer the individual the type of stabilization he needs; nor do they reward efficiency or good management or allow farmers true protection in the case of individual disaster. All across Canada there are problems such as brucellosis or IBR in cattle and various diseases in poultry and hogs which cannot be covered under an aggregate plan but which could be covered under this individual type of plan. We can have a significant price drop in one commodity in western Canada, such as, for example, in barley or rapeseed, but because of the importance of wheat in the western grain stabilization plan the price drop will not trigger aggregate plans; so again these farmers will suffer.
That is why it is imperative in these times of the fluctuating dollar, inflation, world conflicts, rising input costs and increasing consumer resistance to rising food costs that we study and implement an individual stabilization plan. I believe that the committee should start by examining thoroughly the very excellent study that was done by Peat, Marwick and Partners for the Alberta department of agriculture entitled "Feasibility of an Income Averaging Trust Account". The objectives of this plan were that farmers deposit a portion of their income during high revenue years and withdraw funds in lower income years. The main objective was to stabilize the income of the individual farmers on a voluntary basis and at the same time provide indirect stabilization for rural and general economies.
The study outlines a number of concepts with which I totally agree. There are eight of them; that the minimum deposit be one year and the maximum deposit be seven years; that minimum deposits and withdrawals be SI,000 and the maximum amount of the total deposit be $100,000; that in the years that money is withdrawn, no deposits could be made; that only farmers between the age of 18 and 70 would be

Farm Income Stabilization
eligible; that participation in the trust account would be voluntary; that only income from farming operations would be eligible; and that withdrawals would be considered non-farm income and could not be used for block averaging.
They have laid down the basis on which an individual plan could work through a great deal of study and by talking with farm organizations and farmers about what they think they need. I spoke with the unifarm people in Alberta and found them to be in total agreement that we should study the plan as the ultimate stabilization plan for farmers. The impact of the study is to help stabilize the rural economy in the price of farm supplies. This would benefit medium, large and small farmers alike, and in addition it would be of benefit to the government taxation department because revenues from farm income would tend to fluctuate less.
The study has helped us as well because it encompassed all stabilization plans that were available in various countries of the world and concluded that a plan which is now available in New Zealand best fits the idea put forward by the Alberta department of agriculture and studied by Peat, Marwick and Partners. The New Zealand plan has been in place since 1965 and is known as the farm income stabilization scheme. It allows farmers to deposit up to 25 per cent of their gross income into income equalization accounts. The concept of the plan is quite similar to what I have just outlined.
I should like to state in conclusion that here is an opportunity for members of parliament to improve farm income through individual stabilization by passing this motion. The ancillary effects on the total agricultural economy, levels of inventories, farm equipment and supply purchase patterns and the smoothing out of federal and provincial taxation incomes are all important and tend to create an environment where planning and production management techniques could become more effective. In future this plan, with more study, could replace the western grain stabilization plan and the agricultural stabilization plan by having regional triggers in place wherein producer accounts would be supplemented by government payments and producers in various commodity groups would get stabilization help from federal assistance, as is now the case under the western grain stabilization plan, through their individual accounts.
I thank the House for giving me the opportunity to put this motion before hon. members and I hope they give it their serious consideration.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF INSTITUTING INDIVIDUAL INCOME STABILIZATION PROGRAM FOR WESTERN PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) for his motion. I must say in support of the hon. member that I had often the opportunity to meet him during the two years when I was parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture, and his contribution to the Standing Committee on Agriculture was always of the highest standing.
This motion, Mr. Speaker, also indicates that the hon. member is much interested in agriculture. I must admit that
[Mr. Schellenberger. 1
even, as I have just said, if I had the honour to serve as parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture, there are very few farmers in my constituency. There is, of course, the experimental farm of Lennoxville which, I must say, has substantially contributed to the promotion of agriculture in Canada, performing very important research work and serving with outstanding diligence the farmers of Quebec and of the Eastern Townships.
Of course, even if there are not many farmers in my riding, God knows that agriculture and every other aspect of the food industry affects everybody. In the speech he has just made, the hon. member raised some very interesting points which should be taken into serious consideration. However, I should remind hon. members that the Department of Agriculture helped farmers tremendously in the last few years. Take, for example, the two extremely important pieces of legislation which were passed by the House during the last six years, and which were greatly supported by hon. members on the opposition side, and particularly by the mover of the motion which is before us today.
Mr. Speaker, I also want to mention one of his colleagues, the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) who always made a remarkable contribution in the Committee on Agriculture which demonstrates that he is particularly concerned with the agricultural segment of our society and with the interests of his constituents.
Mr. Speaker, the markets are a lot more unstable in agriculture than in most other sectors of the economy. Therefore, the income levels of farmers vary much more than those of other Canadians. This greater uncertainty is a source of great difficulty for farmers and very often slows down the development of agriculture. The inputs and outputs of resources from the production sector, depending on price fluctuations, result in higher production costs.
On the other hand, farmers may be persuaded to renounce certain monetary advantages of specialization, for by varying their crops, they may count on a more stable income and attenuate some of the risks resulting from the slowing down of a market due to the application of modern technology. The climate of uncertainty in which producers live quickly spreads to their suppliers of goods and services and their purchasers of farm products. Finally, their effects are felt on the economy as a whole. Because of the problems resulting from the instability of farm markets, the House has finally adopted stabilization legislation for wheat and other grains.
The programs applied under these two pieces of legislation lessen the effects of unstable markets by ensuring that, during more difficult times, producers will receive support payments which increase their incomes to a level which represents a certain percentage of the net eligible grain sale proceeds for all producers for the year under review. That is exactly what the hon. member who has introduced this motion claimed a while
February 26, 1979

ago. Since the computation of the support level takes these proceeds into account, Canadian farmers will continue, as indeed they should, to base their decisions concerning production on the fundamental tendencies of the prices on the market place.
Mr. Speaker, the stabilization mechanism gives good protection to the farmers against the fluctuations mentioned by the hon. member, but it has much less influence on permanent decreases in market prices since these influence the support levels. All producers receive the same supplementary payment by production unit under these two stabilization programs, this aims at ensuring that the position of each farmer in relation to the others is not changed by the stabilization program.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about the Agricultural Stabilization Act. Even though the programs established under this act have remained within the spirit of the previous act, passed in 1957 or 1958, certain changes have been made to the policy to meet the new requirements of farmers. The first act included provisions for designated products. These were products which had to be supported at a level set at 80 per cent of the average market price in the last ten years or the ten previous years. The government was empowered to increase this minimum level it deemed appropriate. However, non-designated products could benefit from support if need be, but always at the discretion of the minister. The support price of these designated products was equivalent to the ten-year average percentage judged appropriate to absorb losses on the market. The amendments which resulted in the 1975 act have been very beneficial for the farmers. The amendments concern mostly the list of designated products and the formula for establishing the support prices.
Certain designated products were not listed in the 1958 act, and this shows the significant improvements which were made in the new legislation. For instance, the designated products now include steers, pigs, sheep, industrial milk and cream, corn, soya, as well as oats and barley produced outside the zone designated by the Canadian Wheat Board. The minimum support level for these products was set at 90 per cent of the market price during the previous five years.
This is the major difference between the legislation passed in 1958 and that passed in 1975. In the first case, the support level was set at 80 per cent of the prices during the previous ten years, while the support level is now based on a five-year period, which is much more reasonable and much more advantageous for the farmers. In other words, instead of 80 per cent, it is 90 per cent of the last five years. The minimum rate has thus been increased by 10 per cent and the period considered has been lowered from ten to five years. Just as the 1958 act, the revised legislation provides the increase, if need be, of the minimum rate of assistance and the designation of other products for assistance purposes. And we can add to that the problems pertaining to the present agricultural products stabilization program. Also, we all know that apart from this legislation there were the two acts I mentioned in the beginning, namely one on stabilization and one on wheat.
Farm Income Stabilization
The implementation of the 1975 act has brought to light a certain number of problems, namely that some producers consider the rate of assistance too low. In that respect, I think, as the hon. member mentioned about midway through his speech, this deserved some consideration in certain instances, and I believe that the government did indeed, two or three times, increase the amount of assistance granted for certain products. But there again I agree with the hon. member that in certain cases it is clearly too low because imports, that is certain products that cost a lot more in the farmer end product, are not always included. For a lot of producers, not disclosing the support price before the production period also contributes to reduce considerably the extent to which programs lessen the climate of uncertainty.
Cow calves are not on the list of specified products and it is perhaps a lack that should be corrected. A number of pork and cattle producers feel the present program does not protect them adequately and they have to reduce the support period. Here again, producers of these two commodities expressed on several occasions-and I remember on two occasions at the Department of Agriculture-certain claims they felt the government should consider.
Although the legislation included provisions for an increase in the basic rate and its financing by producers no procedures were developed for that purpose. There again, although those two pieces of legislation are in the interest of farmers I believe certain amendments could be brought in, and, of course, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is always prepared to change the existing laws to suit them to current conditions.
Mr. Speaker, I know for having worked with our Minister of Agriculture-who incidentally has been there for seven years-how farmers both in western and eastern Canada appreciate the interest and constant concern he has to fight both at the caucus as well as the ministers' level to ensure farmers get the most and are protected against inflation and certain other economic difficulties. We all know that farmers or agriculturists are perhaps the most vulnerable class in our society because, in addition to the difficulties every group faces, they have to live with the uncertainties of the weather over which they have no control; that is why this government passed legislation to protect them a bit more against bad weather, both literally and figuratively.
Since the act, as amended in 1975, has come into effect, a number of provinces, Mr. Speaker, as should be pointed out here, have adopted their own stabilization programs. Still, the federal government is concerned about the variety of programs implemented with regard to goods produced and sold throughout Canada, because varying levels of support from one province to the other could be a source of numerous problems.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, the federal government does not disagree with the fact that some of the provinces have decided to give help to agriculture. What it is concerned about is the diversity of those programs. Some provinces being richer, they can offer much more than other provinces; consequently, there

February 26, 1979
Farm Income Stabilization
are two classes of farmers in Canada. That is why the Minister of Agriculture has always taken great care to avoid such differences as much as possible. There are enough regional disparities in Canada as it is, which of course we are trying to remedy, but incentives however should not be provided through programs that vary so much from one province to another, although they are valid in themselves. The constant goal of the Minister of Agriculture has been that all those programs help farmers equally across Canada. This is why federal programs have tried to integrate most of the stabilization programs as much as possible and to the extent provinces are willing.
Because each province wants to protect farmers, there could be a run on levels of support, and producers in more generous provinces would naturally have an edge on their counterparts in other provinces, and production could slide to more generous provinces. It is my view and indeed the view of farmers, as will be recognized by the mover of the motion, that with such a range of programs we could eventually get to the point where some provinces could, by reason of their location, economic base and a host of other factors, stimulate producers through generous and acceptable measures into raising their production to a level that would harm producers in other areas, and although this could have short-term benefits for a small number, it certainly would be harmful on the longer term both to themselves and farmers throughout the country. For that reason, federal programs must work across the land and be as generous as possible, while avoiding that some provinces benefit more than others.
On the other hand, this country could get into difficulty with its trading partners, who look badly toward what they feel is unfair subsidizing of Canadian products. The Canadian government and provinces held detailed discussions on all the stabilization programs I referred to. Discussions up till now have been positive, and all parties have been looking for a solution to problems faced by current programs. In the cause of these discussions, a federal-provincial technical committee was created to examine all aspects of the agricultural prices stabilization policy and report to respective ministers. While the present proposal is formulated by the federal government and comes under its responsibility, it was inspired to a large degree by these discussions.
Mr. Speaker, I believe the steps taken over the last six or seven years prove to what pains the federal government, and in particular the present Liberal government and the present Minister of Agriculture, have gone to give not only the agricultural population but all Canadians laws ensuring a greater stability of income for all farmers. This greater stability of income has an impact on all the other economic sectors; one must in fact recognize that if farmers must bear certain difficulties in the agricultural sector, an abnormal increase in food prices may follow. This would of course be due to a lack of planning, to a lack of price stabilization laws on Canadian agricultural products.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I was late getting in at the beginning of this debate, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to make a few remarks in support of my colleague, the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger). He has selected a very worth-while topic which has not received fair comment since the grain stabilization debate of several years ago.
There is much to be said in support of the individual stabilization approach. I think we should give it serious attention. In these few minutes, Mr. Speaker, I want to speak of the special needs it would serve in the drought areas across southern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan where there are the resultant extremes in farm and ranch income. This is materially affected by the rapid sales of livestock, grain and farm products due to the drought conditions which are a fact of life in that area.
I should like to give two excellent examples of this, Mr. Speaker, the years 1977 and 1978. The 1977 records show it was the worst single drought year since the 1930s. I speak with some conviction, Mr. Speaker, because I remember those years. The worst years were 1931, 1932 and 1937. The year 1977 was at least the equal in terms of growth, or lack of it, to those years in the thirties. Surface water, of course, is the staff of life in those drought areas, but snow run-off during that single year was worse than at any time in the ten-year period.
In sharp contrast, 1978 was one of the best growth years. I would go as far as to say it was the best growth year for natural grass or hay since 1927. The growth of cultivated grains was above average but not as spectacular in 1978 as was the growth of grass and hay.
Such extremes of moisture conditions present real problems to people involved in agriculture. I think we should give some special recognition to this problem when we discuss a stabilization program. The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton) drew attention to the need for special recognition of these extremes in committee when we were considering the grain stabilization bill several years ago and he proposed the same concept-that it should be handled on an individual basis. I suggest that in the rush to stabilize various agricultural commodities this more practical and sensible approach has been completely overlooked. The hon. member for Wetaskiwin pointed out that the proposal has been fully researched by the planning and research secretariat of the Alberta department of agriculture. I do not wish to promote
February 26, 1979

this type of program for just that province, however, as I think there should be national individual stabilization.
In fairness, Mr. Speaker, I should say that most of my remarks will probably be directed to the possibility of such a program being used in the Canadian beef cattle industry but the same concept could apply to any other agricultural commodity. The basic concept of the individual approach would be that a farmer could deposit a portion of his income during high income years and withdraw some or all of those funds during low income years, in effect creating his own stabilization program. This has some basic advantages over what could be termed a universal stabilization plan, the concept that we have been considering officially until now.
Amongst the advantages, first of all, is the fact that it should cost less to the public treasury in terms of payout and the bureaucracy-needed to administer it. Second, the tax payments of farmers would probably not be greatly affected. They might increase as a result of a more stable environment, and tax revenues would tend to even out over the years which would be a good thing. The third advantage, and perhaps the most important, is that the plan would not obscure market signals in any way, whereas a universal plan tends to insulate farmers from the realities of the marketplace. That is most important, especially in the cattle industry. The feeling that goes along with that insulation from the marketplace is that if the market place does not pay enough, the taxpayer will. That feeling does exist as a result of the way some stabilization programs have been operated.
The fourth advantage that I see is that it would discourage farmers from attempting to delay taxes by maximizing costs in high income years. A big example of this is the practice of feeders and cattlemen of purchasing feeder cattle near the year end and carrying them over for resale in the next taxation year. This distorts the cattle market, and we are better off without such a practice. An individual stabilization program would get around this problem.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, the program suggested by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin has much to commend it over the current guaranteed margin approach that the federal government suggests in its new look at the stabilization program. What disturbs me about this program is the suggestion that there be a 100 per cent support level. That is what used to be called "top loading." A 100 per cent margin approach will guarantee a real top loaded situation. The danger of this is that it will definitely lead to overproduction. We would be ignorant of our immediate past history if we did not remember what led us into the situation we find ourselves in now where we have the highest prices in the history of the cattle industry because of the situation developed with an oversupply, influenced by government policies four or five years ago.
A stabilization program is fine, but we should not go overboard with it and then find ourselves in the situation that would require production controls. That would not be received very favourably by cattlemen. Those are my comments, Mr. Farm Income Stabilization
Speaker. I am very pleased to be here to support my colleague, the hon. member for Wetaskiwin.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF INSTITUTING INDIVIDUAL INCOME STABILIZATION PROGRAM FOR WESTERN PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to participate for a few moments in this particular debate. I am always happy to listen to both hon. members who have put forward their thoughts with respect to farm income and agriculture from the opposite side, namely, the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) and the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave).
Let me say that I only disagreed with one comment made by the member from Medicine Hat when in essence, perhaps inadvertently he attributed some of the difficulties that the cattle industry in Canada and around the world has gone through over the last several years to government policies. I know my hon. friend is well aware that it would not matter if we had had no cattle in either Alberta or Saskatchewan over the last few years, we would still have seen more or less the same erratic fluctuations which have occurred in the United States, Australia, Brazil, and so on. We were not alone in some of the misjudgments, if you like, that were involved in terms of the very high numbers, which then decreased. We are now in a situation where the prices are up. I know his constituents and mine are more than happy with the prices being received today for beef and beef cattle. But consumers put pressure on provincial and federal governments, not only in Canada but elsewhere, to look at this whole question again to see what can

February 26, 1979
Farm Income Stabilization
or cannot be done. I share many of his views with respect to what can be done and what cannot be done, as well.
I would only quarrel with one aspect of the motion today, although I quarrel very little with the thoughts and thesis in general put forward by hon. members opposite. The motion reads:
That the Standing Committee on Agriculture be empowered to study the advisability of instituting an individual rather than aggregate program of income stabilization for the western producer-
My quarrel is with the "rather than" idea. I do not believe we can divorce the two concepts. I do not believe we can say there is no need for over-all farming stabilization plans, programs or policies, whether this pertains to potatoes, grain, beef, milk or anything else. Maybe we could look at some improvement and some changes in present policy, and perhaps present tax legislation to accommodate some of the things referred to, particularly as it pertains to the beef industry in western Canada. This was spelled out just a few moments ago by the hon. member for Medicine Hat. However, I would point out again my basic disagreement with the way the motion is worded, and say I would oppose it on that basis only. I am not opposing many of the excellent points put forward.
If I may take a moment or two to look at the general goals of stabilization plans, whether we are talking west or east it does not matter a great deal, we must look and ask ourselves what a general stabilization plan is designed to do. We should also ask ourselves whether we can devise an individual plan that will meet some of those objectives. I would suggest a stabilization plan for agriculture or for any agricultural product should first of all stabilize the income of the agricultural industry.
Second, it should help to stabilize the agricultural input in the industry. I am thinking here of the fertilizer industry, the chemical industry, veterinary supplies etc., all other machinery and related industries involved in agricultural input.
Third, I suppose an agricultural stabilization program should serve to stabilize the economy of the region. This, as my hon. friends opposite and indeed all members of this House know, has been one of the difficulties in western Canada, the instability of income for everybody in all economic sectors. We do not have to go back to the 1930s to those dramatic times with respect to lack of crops and lack of prices and the devastating effects which that cycle had. We have not seen anything similar to that since, but we still see the ups and downs, and the effects which they have on an entire region.
Then we must look at stability with respect to the income of an individual farmer as well; that I recognize and acknowledge. If we are talking only stability with respect to the individual, as opposed to paying no attention or very little attention to the over-all objectives of a stabilization program, we are not meeting all of the concerns with which we should be dealing.
I am sure that all hon. members in this House who are from farming areas particularly know of the high prices and high costs of input, the kinds of dollars and figures which farmers have to deal with today in writing cheques and in paying bills,

along with the kinds of receipts which they have to have, the income from any one of the farm products, that all of this is more and more important today than it ever was. Therefore we must look at every possibility of trying to bring about greater stability in the income of the individual farmer, producer, and farm producers collectively.
Cash flow today is absolutely vital to farmers in terms of continuing to operate. It does not matter whether they are maritime potato growers, or beef producers or grain growers. Long gone are the days when one could get by on a farm, as I did in the maritimes when I was growing up, with very little cash income. At that time one could also grow crops and bring them in and manage to get by with very few dollars. But that day has long since gone in all regions of the country and in all sectors of agriculture.
We need to look at our present aggregate plans. We need to stress those over and above the individual concept and the points made by my hon. friends in this particular motion. An aggregate plan will stabilize the income of the industry by making payouts when the income of that industry decreases. We have seen an example of that just in the past year with respect to the western grain stabilization program. I recall some of the questions and issues which came forward from that very good session of the committee at that time, referred to by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin.
The plan is now in operation. It is quite likely there will be a payout in that plan in the current year. He is correct in this sense that it does not meet all of the individual requirements that may come along. I am not sure that it should. I worry about a plan looking after the individual's cash needs in terms of having more interference with what that farmer may do or may not do. As the hon. member knows, in his part of Alberta, and in my part of Saskatchewan, the cereal grain farmer can grow wheat, or barley, or flax-he can grow a number of things in most cases. If we tied it up too much on an individual crop basis-

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF INSTITUTING INDIVIDUAL INCOME STABILIZATION PROGRAM FOR WESTERN PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Order, please. The hour reserved for consideration of private members' business having expired, I do now leave the chair until eight o'clock.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.
February 26, 1979

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Ouellet that Bill C-29, to amend the National Housing Act and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act and to make other related amendments, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
Mir. Art Lee (Vancouver East): Mr. Speaker, before the five o'clock adjournment I was addressing myself to the amendments with respect to the RRAP program. I indicated at that time that the RRAP program in effect had its origins in an area of my constituency known as Strathcona. I believe it is then appropriate for me to retell the Strathcona story in order that all hon. members can understand the significance of rehabilitation.
Strathcona is one of Vancouver's oldest residential neighbourhoods. Most of the houses in the area were built about the turn of the century, but some date back to the origins of the city itself. The Strathcona school was originally built in 1890 as the East End school.
The early residents of Strathcona were Anglo-Saxon. However, the area soon became inhabited by large numbers of Italians and Jews, as well as Scandinavians, Ukrainians, Russians and Yugoslavs. The old Hastings Auditorium at 828 East Hastings used to be called the "Italian Hall" and was the centre of Vancouver's pre-World War II Italian community. Benny's Italian Market at Union and Princess dates back to 1915. The Gibbs Boys Club building at Heatley and Pender was originally built in 1921 as the Schara Tzedeck Synagogue. The Ukrainian Canadian Centre at Hawks and Pender dates back to 1928. The church at Princess and Pender was built as the Swedish Lutheran Church and served as the Ukrainian Catholic Church before it became the Chinese Catholic Church. The Russian People's Home on Campbell Avenue, adjacent to the Russian Orthodox Church, was built by the Yugoslav community. The Yugoslavs had their own centre on Keefer Street.
Compared to the Europeans, the Chinese were latecomers to Strathcona. There were some Chinese and Japanese living in the area in the 1930s. However, it was not until after the repeal of the Chinese Exclusion Act in 1947 that Strathcona became increasingly Chinese. The area served as a gateway for postwar Chinese immigrants. Housing prices were low and the area was adjacent to Chinatown.
In 1947 Strathcona was only about 28 per cent Chinese. By 1957 this figure had reached about 50 per cent. Strathcona today is about 75 per cent Chinese. It contains less than 10 per cent of greater Vancouver's 60,000-plus Chinese. There are large numbers of Chinese living in neighbourhoods well outside of the Chinatown-Strathcona area.
Housing
In 1957 the city of Vancouver embarked upon a 20-year urban renewal plan. A major focus of this program was comprehensive redevelopment for Strathcona, the clearance of all existing homes and replacement with public housing, high rises, and row housing. Union Street was to be the southern border of the new Strathcona as the blocks of homes below it were to be demolished for a major city freeway system.
The rationale for the urban renewal was that Strathcona, in addition to having old and rundown housing, was in a strategic location being adjacent to the downtown, waterfront and False Creek areas. The city wanted high density development for Strathcona. Commencing in 1958, the city placed a freeze upon the entire area; property values were frozen; no major redevelopment and home improvement permits were allowed, and no regular public works maintenance was carried out. The neighbourhood was left to await the bulldozer.
The first phase of urban renewal began in 1959 with the construction of 159 units of public housing at MacLean Park. An entire block of homes was then demolished as a new replacement park. Ten acres of land and homes were then cleared in preparation for the 376 unit Raymur Place housing project at Campbell Avenue.
Acquisition and clearance for Scheme II urban renewal began in 1965 with the expropriation and clearance of homes in five blocks for an extention to MacLean Park, senior citizens housing, and an extention to Strathcona school.
The urban renewal schemes met strong opposition from Strathcona residents and Chinatown leaders. It was pointed out that the urban renewal would destroy the community and threaten the livelihood of Chinatown. The expropriation of homes for $6,000-$8,000 was argued to be unfair and discriminatory. The protests were of no avail as the city continued with its urban renewal. In August, 1968, the city prepared Scheme III, the final and complete bulldozing of the entire neighbourhood. Fortunately this scheme was never implemented as the federal government reassessed its urban renewal involvement across Canada.
The third and final urban renewal proposal had also sparked a last ditch effort among Strathcona residents to stop the bulldozing of their neighbourhood. In December, 1968, 600 persons attended the founding meeting of the Strathcona Property Owners and Tenants Association, SPOTA. The purpose of the new organization was to ensure that the people who live in the area would be fully informed, and their interests and community would be protected. In briefs to city hall, SPOTA argued for a revised renewal scheme which favoured rehabilitation and preservation.
In the fall of 1969 SPOTA was asked by the senior governments to join in a four level committee to investigate rehabilitation for Strathcona. It was the first time in Canada that a committee had been charged with that responsibility. It was also the first time that a citizens group had been invited to participate in such a capacity.

February 26, 1979
Housing
In July, 1971, after almost two years of meetings, studies and negotiations, the committee agreed upon a series of recommendations. They called for a $4.9 million rehabilitation scheme, with two million dollars each in new public works and grant-loan housing rehabilitation assistance. The Strathcona rehabilitation project officially began in February, 1972, and operated out of a site office on Hawks Avenue. During the three years of implementation, the three levels of government, site office staff and the community worked closely and informally together.
In the summer of 1973 the federal government introduced national programs for neighbourhood improvement and rehabilitation based largely on the Strathcona experience. The new programs, NIP and RRAP, which the city of Vancouver has already chosen for certain areas, include additional and expanded features of the Strathcona project. The new programs are also meant to recognize a meaningful role for citizen involvement in the neighbourhood improvement process.
With the completion of the rehabilitation project in 1975, Strathcona displays a new look and spirit. Under the project 233 houses were improved, with the majority of home owners expending sums above and beyond the grant-loan assistance. If the original $2 million allotted for housing rehabilitation assistance, less than $700,000 was spent. This resulted because the grant-loan scheme excluded more home owners and failed to attract more landlords than had originally been estimated. The new sidewalks, sewers and streets were installed but overran their $2 million budget by $500,000.
With strong community initiative, a new linear park was funded by the rehabilitation project. Vacant lots were used in the park development to connect the existing parks in the neighbourhood. The linear park also involved blocking off streets and thus curtailing heavy truck and non-residential traffic through the community.
Another worth-while development during the rehabilitation project was the home improvement centre. Initiated by Strathcona students, this centre offered free design services and home improvement, and operated repair workshops for the elderly and lower income people. It operated under OFY and LIP funding.
For members of SPOTA, rehabilitation of their neighbourhood did not end with the rehabilitation project. Midway through the project in 1973, SPOTA initiated plans for nonprofit housing on infill lots throughout their neighbourhood. These lots, which had been acquired by the city under urban renewal, were sold to the provincial government at SPOTA's request. The province was to lease the land for non-profit housing.
SPOTA began its housing program with a seven-unit cooperative on five vacant lots at 730 Union Street. After several months of delay by city zoning officials, the project began construction in the fall of 1974. Five months later the seven families moved in. Financing of the co-operative came under the federal government's non-profit housing program.
In the fall of 1975 SPOTA began phase two of the infill housing. This involved three units of housing on double lots at eight different Strathcona locations. The first families started moving into the new units in the spring of 1976. Financing for this phase came under the provincial government's non-profit housing program.
The third and final phase of the infill housing involves the construction of single units on 16 remaining small lots. Construction was to begin in the summer of 1976.
Future SPOTA housing plans include non-profit housing on the vacant land opposite the Strathcona school. This site was acquired by the city under urban renewal and then sold to a developer for $210,000, about one third of the cost of the land assembly. In 1971 the city sought to buy it back for three times the amount to locate a large firehall there. After strong Strathcona-Chinatown protests, which culminated in a large rally in December, 1972, civic officials re-declared the land for housing. In February, 1974, SPOTA and another organization were chosen by the city to develop non-profit and senior citizens housing on the site. Although the two organizations submitted detailed housing plans to the city in the fall of 1974, no city action has been taken because of a legal suit filed by the private developer demanding market value for the land. At the present time the "firehall site" is a parking lot operated for and by the Vancouver police department.
During its years of existence, SPOTA has not only been involved in rehabilitation and new housing, but has also been concerned with many other community matters. The organization has worked closely with other Strathcona groups in social services and recreational and educational concerns. The orani-zation has participated in many festivals and conferences which have taken place in the area. It has assisted students and researchers interested in neighbourhood improvement and rehabilitation.
For SPOTA neighbourhood improvement will not end with the rehabilitation project and the new housing. It is a continuous process. Other problems will be encountered.
Whatever the future, there has been one central principle throughout the Strathcona experience, and that is that citizens must participate in those decisions which affect their community. This principle has been fought for by SPOTA, as it has been by many other neighbourhood organizations across Canada.
Also, Mr. Speaker, I have three other designated NIP/ RRAP areas in my riding, these being the downtown eastside, Grandview-Woodlands, and Kiwassa. I also share, with my hon. friend from Vancouver-Kingsway, the NIP/RRAP area known as Mount Pleasant. The same success story is applicable to these communities, People living in these areas have pride. They feel they belong to a neighbourhood. That is well worth the exercise.
I am told that since the program was introduced in 1973 CMHC has been assisting in the rehabilitation of some 20,000 units a year. I hope that as the program is broadened, and as municipal officials become more familiar with its application,
[Mr. Lee.1
February 26, 1979

we will be able to increase that annual rate. It is important to bear in mind, however, that residential rehabilitation is a long-term program.
There are some two million housing units in Canada which were built before the end of the World War II. Some of these are in good shape, and some are now beyond rehabilitation. A great many of them-perhaps as many as half of these old houses-could benefit from some basic rehabilitation and have their useful life extended by a number of years. The point I would like to make is that a job of this magnitude cannot be accomplished overnight, or even in a single year. The number of homes that can be rehabilitated in any year depends not only upon the federal funds which can be made available but also upon the capacity of municipal organizations to manage and implement the program, and on availability of skilled, organized manpower to carry out the actual repairs and reconstruction. There is no question that residential rehabilitation will continue in Canada and will grow year by year.
There is no doubt in my mind either that the Government of Canada will continue to play a leadership role in this growing industry. The critical importance of rehabilitation is becoming more widely recognized every day in Canada and throughout the world.
More and more people are recognizing the importance of saving housing and extending its useful life, instead of tearing it down and building something new. Rehabilitation and preservation are part of the whole philosophy of the conserver society. There is a need to manage and recycle our non-renewable resources.
If we can make our existing housing work longer, there is a very significant saving in energy, materials, and financial resources, compared with starting from scratch to build new houses. This trend is an important part of the changing pattern of housing development which is emerging in Canada and throughout the world. It means that our concerns are gradually shifting away from annual production targets to a broader concept of housing needs.
Since the end of World War II and up until recent years our main concern has been with production, the generation of new housing starts. CMHC was established in 1946 to help us catch up with the backlog of housing production created by the depression and the war years. We were worried, first of all, about housing for returning veterans, and then about the growing demand created by the so-called baby boom. The production of new housing was a critical problem in those years and has continued to be important. Many of our National Housing Act programs have been intended to encourage new construction. Up to now, that has been our prime goal.
Times are changing, however, and so are our housing needs. The rate of population growth has been slowing down for the last 20 years or so and this likely will continue for at least another decade. This fact and others mean that we will need less new housing each year. By the mid-eighties, as we have all read, we will probably need only about 200,000 starts a year.
Housing
Declining population growth also means that there will be a higher proportion of elderly people in the population. At the same time, more people are putting off getting married and having children. Young people are leaving home at an earlier age. The result of these trends will be smaller households and more so-called non-family households. The net effect of all these changes will be a shift from the suburbs, away from the ranch bungalows and family-type, child-oriented housing, toward the inner city where housing is older and more in need of rehabilitation.
The rising cost of fuel and our dwindling energy resources will, of course, accelerate this shift into the city proper by raising the cost of the daily journey to work.
All the demographic trends, economic projections and our shifting social values suggest that rehabilitation is going to be a more significant activity for at least the rest of this century. I am pleased to see the government, in bringing forward these amendments, recognizes the importance of rehabilitation and conservation and has reaffirmed its intention to continue to support it in a tangible way.
One particular amendment relating to rehabilitation deserves special mention, namely, the lifting of the $500 forgiveness feature on private rooming houses. The rate will be established by regulation and therefore this method provides the required flexibility. At present, the law provides for loans up to $4,000 per bed to rehabilitate rooming houses with $500 of this amount being forgivable. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) recognized this as being totally inadequate, and these amendments take care of this by removing the maximum ceiling of $500.
What does this mean, however, in human terms? Really, it finally recognizes that people who live in the downtown cores of cities, often wrongly referred to as skid rows, are entitled to decent housing, as well as those who live in more affluent areas.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
The seed for this amendment was planted during the Habitat conference which took place in Vancouver in the spring of 1976 when the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) visited the downtown east side of Vancouver in his former capacity as minister of state for urban affairs. He saw the deplorable conditions first-hand. The same is true in other Canadian cities, like Toronto. Unfortunately, the conditions in Vancouver's downtown east side are indescribable with words, but let me illustrate by quoting from a report entitled "The Downtown East Side Report" as follows:
In general, though, the relevant area is bounded by Clark Drive, Cambie Street, the south lane of Hastings Street, and the waterfront. It also includes a number of hotels and rooming houses in Chinatown and Strathcona. A number of people live in a similar housing situation in the downtown core, particularly on Granville Street, but because of resource limitations they were not specifically included in the study.
Over the past few decades, accommodation in hotels and rooming houses has been allowed to decline in both quantity and quality. Commercial uses and office space uses have pushed many residents eastward, first out of the downtown core, and, later, out of the Gastown area. Residents have opposed this trend, but

February 26, 1979
Housing
municipal zoning policies have allowed it to continue. More recently, re-zoning proposals threaten to allow industrial uses to displace residential accommodation in the Oppenheimer area, east of Main Street. New zoning policies to stabilize and reinforce the residential character of the area would be needed to halt this over-all trend.
The hotels involved are very old buildings, some of them built before the turn of the century. The above-ground floors are divided into single rooms. Usually, the ground floor contains commercial space, often premises with a liquor licence legally supported by the rooms upstairs. The rooming houses are smaller buildings or large older houses divided into separate rooms for tenants.
For years the hotels and rooming houses of the downtown eastside have been characterized by an almost continuous stream of complaints about uncleanliness, pests, fire hazards, etc. These conditions usually violate Vancouver bylaw standards. The problem has been not that the standards are too lenient, but that the standards have not been met, in practice.
In fact the report disclosed that the total number of bylaw violations found in the 23 buildings examined was 9,743.
What about the people who live in these rooming houses? Who are they? Putting the sex, age and household status of the tenants together, the most typical tenant interviewed was a 50 to 59-year old man living by himself.
Because the area involved is wrongfully referred to as skid row, there is a myth that tenants who live there are transient. In fact the average length of residence is about 13 years, an astonishing figure for a neighbourhood that has a reputation as a transient area. This result is confirmed by the 1971 census, which showed that the downtown east side is the second most stable residential area of Vancouver, after Dunbar, a comfortable single family dwelling area.
With respect to income, it is striking that almost all the people surveyed receive well below the minimum income estimated by the Canadian Senate as necessary for a decent, healthy life in Canada; 34 per cent receive less than half the poverty level. In short, most of the tenants are on fixed incomes, receiving guaranteed income supplements, war veterans allowances, Canada Pension and unemployment insurance. With this particular amendment, rehabilitation of these rooming houses can now go ahead. Rehabilitation will unquestionably help this area, but new housing is also required. The federal government, through CMHC, considers new housing a priority in this area. What does the city of Vancouver say? His Worship Jack Volrich says it is not a priority area.
What does the province say? Well, it is up to the city to declare its priority and, in any event, the province will not make direct subsidies available to new housing projects, other than senior citizens' projects. Clearly, given the level of incomes in this area, subsidies are required to augment and to ensure the amendments in this current bill regarding social housing will be effective. However, the city and the province through the minister of housing, the hon. William Vander Zalm, who is well known to hon. members of this House for his "Frog" songs-

speechtext:
-are reluctant to reciprocate the federal measures. I submit this is because of ignorance on the part of the present minister of housing in British Columbia and the mayor
[Mr. Lee.)
and city council of Vancouver. To classify this area as skid-row is totally unacceptable. Residents, like other Canadian citizens, deserve decent, affordable housing. The federal minister of housing has recognized this by these amendments, and I would encourage the city of Vancouver and the province of British Columbia to join with the federal government in helping areas like the downtown east side core of the city of Vancouver.
We are dealing with human beings, not some mythical notion of skid-row bums or winos. To allow areas like the downtown east side to stagnate because of ignorance would be a travesty and a condemnation of modern civilization.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order which is directed to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Lee), having listened to his very lengthy but very informative speech. I find myself in a similar position in my riding. What can we do as members of parliament here in Ottawa to get rid of the slum landlords, to try to get rid of the people who would take-

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. In answer to the question the hon. member put to me about what we can do with absentee and slum landlords, let me say to him that the first thing we can do in the city of Vancouver-and some members of the council in that city have been trying to do it-is to get the city standards and bylaws enforced. If you start enforcing these bylaws, it is argued these people will close the hotels and the private rooming houses. But our experience has shown that this is not necessarily the case.
The more recent experience we have had in the area of enforcing the bylaw with respect to the installation of fire sprinklers cost a lot of money, and most of the absentee landlords said they would have to close these premises down because of the cost. But the enforcement of these bylaws has saved a number of lives and has not resulted in most of these absentee landlords closing down the premises. A lot has to be done by the maintenance of city standards and bylaws, but the kinds of amendments envisaged in this legislation will help as well.
