Mr. Speaker, it is Monday, February 26, 1979, and I want you to know, sir, that in the House of Commons, in the nation's capital, things are as they ought to be. We on this side propose and they on the other side oppose. We have taken the stance of the government in proposing the positive proposals on the deductibility of interest on property taxes. They on the other side are preparing
February 26, 1979

themselves for the opposition and are taking the stance of opposing that.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Just listen to those Liberals howl. The minister leading off the debate and his Liberals have spent more time criticizing and attacking the Conservative proposal and policy, which is a clear, popular policy across the country, of interest deductibility of municipal property taxes. The minister spoke in the House for two and a half hours but did not say anything. He is a minister who speaks well in both languages but says nothing in either. For two and a half hours he spoke in this chamber and, by and large, he said nothing except to criticize the PC policy of interest deductibility of municipal property taxes.
You will understand, sir, my reluctance to believe them because I well remember the time back in the election campaign of 1974 when this government and this minister went across the country preaching to the Canadian people, and sounding so sincere, that price and wage controls would not work. I remember well the night when the Prime Minister of this country (Mr. Trudeau) spoke on national television and, in a most dramatic moment, pointed straight to every Canadian and said, "Zap, you're frozen." The Liberals were against wage and price controls, and every Canadian knew they were against it. To a man they were categorically opposed to them. Well, sir, here they sit tonight, as they did yesterday and last week, and as I suppose they will tomorrow, opposed to our program of interest deductibility and municipal tax deductibility from personal income tax. So you will undertstand if I am reluctant to believe them, for these Liberals will change their minds as the wind changes and they will Find out, as they have in the byelections and since, what the people truly think.
They sent a contingent down to Washington to prepare a report and to come back and tell us that everyone in Washington is against our program. If they could, they would undo it. Why, everyone is against it except the people, except the 230 million Americans. Well, sir, my party and I, we will all stay with the people.
I was somewhat impressed by the housing critic of my party, the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott), as she spoke in the House for about an hour. She did not use the kind of biting criticism that was a characteristic of the minister's speech. She was constructive. To that degree I can also compliment the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Lee) because, although his opening remarks in the First Five or ten minutes were critical of our deductibility program, he did at least devote part of his speech to his own riding and the things that are happening there. These Liberals are so preoccupied
and all in a fluff because they are on the wrong side, not only of a good issue but of the right issue. I am going to set them straight and do what, from time to time, is required of students of government who have not done their homework. I will lecture them, sir, from Five to ten minutes on the merits of the interest deductibility proposal.
Housing
First of all, the minister should know that our program is not a housing program. He referred to it time and time again as the Tory housing policy. It is not a housing policy. We have told him and told him, but we will tell him again that this is not our housing policy. Now that the super minister of economic affairs is here, perhaps he might write it down and tape the note in front of his desk so that in time he will understand that this is not our housing policy, it is an economic policy.
Our economic policy on the deductibility of interest on your principal residence up to a maximum of $5,000 a year is based on the principle that governments prejudice interest rates. I am fortunate in that the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras) is in the House paying strict attention, and I am sure that when he speaks on this subject he will underscore the reality that governments, by their borrowing practices and spending habits, in essence set the interest rates of the country. It is because of the wasteful and extravagant spending of the government that the interest rates on first mortgages in this country are anywhere between 11.75 per cent to 12.5 per cent, depending in what part of the country you apply for a mortgage. So the First principle of our program is based on the reality that government sets interest rates.
Then the other reality is that in the 25 or 30-year amortization period of a mortgage, interest constitutes a large portion of the principal and interest mortgage payment.
Another principle upon which our policy is based is that housing is the right of every Canadian. We disagree with what was suggested by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) when he said that housing was a luxury. I do not consider housing to be a luxury. It is the right of every Canadian who wants to own his own home. The government ought to put its Financial affairs into shape so that those Canadians can afford homes. It is with that background that we adopted a policy of interest deductibility. Our policy is a simple one. Its maximum is $5,000 a year on a maximum mortgage of $50,000 on the interest deductibility side. It must be on a principal residence, a First mortgage, and $1,000 maximum property taxes.
We heard the minister and other government members scrambling to think of every conceivable bad point in our policy. They even put the best minds at the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to work. I know my information is true because I was told by members of CMHC. The minister told them to burn the midnight oil. They were told to get their best minds and brains working on getting reasons why the Tory policy is bad and will not work. The minister did not ask for an objective analysis of the deductibility. He wanted reasons to Fire back at Tory members why the program would not work. They came up with the following reasons.
They said our program was for the rich. The facts prove them wrong. There are approximately 4.6 million households in the country. Approximately 67 per cent, or two-thirds, of home owners earn under $15,000, and only 6 per cent earn

February 26, 1979
Housing
over $25,000. The argument that our program is for the rich just does not bear out. As a matter of fact, if one combines all the incomes of people working in a given family, 35 per cent of family incomes are under $10,000. Only 10 per cent of the combined incomes within families owning homes are over $25,000. When the Grits go around the country indicating that it is not a policy for the poor, they do not have the facts, and the facts prove them wrong.
Another great criticism which is mimicked in unison from time to time by hon. members opposite is that there will be a great run on the mortgage market. Canadian mortgage funds will dry up, according to hon. members opposite, if everyone runs out and borrows all the money they can against their homes to take full advantage of the mortgage deductibility scheme. Perhaps that will occur, but we must remember that most Canadians have mortgages on their homes, or those who do not have the maximum possible mortgages on their homes, run out to borrow money in order to take advantage of the scheme, will they put it in cookie jars or their socks? Of course not. They will re-invest it.
The other day my leader coined a phrase, a little slogan which means a lot, "From the sock to the stock." I happen to think Canadians are astute in investing their money in Canada. Thus I am excited about the possibility of Canadians borrowing against their homes to invest in this country. If they do that, our program will be of double benefit to the country.
Also hon. members opposite indicate that our program would discriminate against renters. The minister made a great ado about this. He indicated that our policy would discriminate against renters. I took the time to visit one apartment block in my constituency. I knocked on several doors and said, "Do you have a dream or a hope of one day owning your own home?" In every single case the answer was "Yes". I do not deny from time to time some Canadians prefer to rent, but by and large renters want to own their own homes. Our program would allow their hopes to happen and their dreams to come true. It would allow a large number of renters to own their own homes. The Liberals who suggest this program discriminates against renters should talk to the renters and find out that that is not the case.
Also hon. members opposite have indicated that the government could not afford such a program. They have asked how Tories would be able to pay for the program, and have come up with astronomical figures. We indicated that the cost of the program would be $1.6 billion in the fourth year, and the Liberal government increased that cost by $4 billion. That is the type of Grit financing which has occurred over the last 15 years. We have said that it would cost approximately $1.6 billion, and our estimation will not be out by much. We can afford such a scheme because we believe the Auditor General when he said there was waste and inefficiency in the government. Now we have a political commitment.
When my leader goes across the country talking about zero-based financing, sunset laws, the efficiency of government, and squeezing every tax dollar for every bit of worth we can get out of it, he means it. We are committed to such a
government program, and that is why our interest deductibility scheme will work. Also we know it will work because we have the support of Canadians across the country.
We on this side know the comments that we have been receiving, as well as the comments being received by government members. This is an exciting program which gets the blood of Canadians running. They see tax dollars coming to them which otherwise would go to the government. An increase in their disposable incomes makes them excited because it increases their buying power. That would be an economic stimulus. I suspect there are still Liberals in the country who will attempt to discredit our program every time they get a chance, but they should remember that Canadians are accepting our program and rejecting their criticism. They are lining up by the hundreds of thousands to support a government which proposes such programs.
We are beginning to prepare for governing, while the Liberal government is beginning to prepare itself for the role of opposition. The Liberal government is stale and a spendthrift. It is almost foreshadowing the things to come when the Prime Minister calls the next election.
Other members on this side of the House will deal with various aspects of Bill C-29 which should have been before the House for consideration a year ago. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) should not stand in his place and suggest that we ought to give this bill quick passage, and then speak on it for 2.5 hours one year after it should have been introduced. We on this side will take the bill apart piece by piece. In committee we will reconstruct it so that it will deal effectively with the problems in the country. The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) will deal with AHOP. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) will deal with rural housing and CHIP. The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) will deal with RRAP and community services. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) will deal with native housing, and so on. We on this side will propose such positive amendments and criticisms of this legislation that it will be whipped into shape. In committee we will continue the mentality which the government has displayed in preparing itself for the role of opposition.
I am concerned that Bill C-29 merely begins new directions in housing, a new era in consultation and relations between the federal and provincial governments, a new direction in housing, from public to social and a new era in financing, that is, a shift from the government sector to the private sector. I would like to deal with those three areas.
The era of consultation, of realizations between the federal government and the provincial governments is the first one with which I would like to deal. We have had a decade of intrusion by the federal government into provincial jurisdiction, and as a death repentance, at the last hour on the eve of a federal election the Minister of State for Urban Affairs is scrambling about the country finally realizing that the ministry of state for urban affairs must wind down and get out of

February 26, 1979

areas of jurisdiction belonging to the provinces, so he talks about global funding.
Consultation means to seek opinion and implies obtaining agreement before action is taken. The most recent report of the task force of western premiers on constitutional trends reads at page 31:
In the broad areas of housing and urban affairs, consultation is virtually non existent.
The western premiers have found that through the years consultation has not been there, so when the minister claimed there had been consultation he implied that not only had he sought their advice, that there was discussion on the various courses of action, but that there had been agreement before action was taken. We now have as of January 1, in effect, a new housing act for community services, and yet as of that date there were provinces which had not signed and were not in agreement, but parliament is asked to ratify the amendments.
Parliament, in the tradition which I know it, is a body which debates the proposals of the federal government before they are implemented, but in this case we are asked merely to ratify the decision already made and implemented by the federal government. I can see, in looking at the documentation which I can Find, and hearing the testimony of the provinces, that this was a hurried move by the minister. There were two meetings, one of which was on February 1, 1978, in Edmonton. After those two meetings, and without agreement, the minister decides unilaterally on a new direction for housing, the new community service program, and he is chopping AHOP, changing RRAP, and abolishing ARP and all the rest, on a unilateral decision by this government. That certainly is not consultation. That is a new direction in housing, but it is a typical kind of consultation which characterizes this government.
What we now see is more central housing policies in the name of unity and that the provincial governments are now asked not to be co-makers of policy or co-determiners of a direction for housing, but to be nothing more than administrators, the boys who do the leg work for the kinds of programs envisaged by the minister. For those who believe that this federal government consults with the provinces about global funding, I would read to hon. members what the minister said in his speech as it is reported at page 3551 of Hansard:
This bill will enable us not only to reach our goals in the housing field but also to obtain an even wider objective. It will enable the government to co-operate with other government levels so that Canadians may live in a safe and pleasant environment.
He goes on to say a few lines down:
The community services program was discussed with the provincial ministers concerned.
Perhaps it was discussed, but there was no agreement reached and nothing signed before it was implemented. He then goes on to say:
The federal government will continue, of course, to provide help in the form of direct grants for all those activities but it will extend from now on its assistance to a whole list of social, cultural and recreational services.
Housing
This minister is not only continuing the tradition of this government of intrusion into provincial rights respecting housing, but in fact he is enlarging his share of influence. By the minister's own definition this program now covers a whole list of social, cultural, and recreational services. I can see that this new era of consultation is really a new era of intrusion by this federal minister, under the hoax of community services and the illusion of global funding. I like his language because it sounds good, but he betrays himself as to what he really means. I am concerned that this new era of consultation is really much more widespread in terms of intrusion, but as far as the mentality of the minister is concerned, it is only business as usual.
This bill poses a new era in the direction of housing from the public sector to the social sector. I have been watching the clock and it must be on "speed up" time because it is just flying by, so I am going to make one point and then go on to a solution I have for the minister which I would like to put to him before my time expires. We see in this shift from public to social housing-and by that I mean a new concept in the thinking of this minister and this government-that the responsibility of the federal government is not simply providing the unity which is a classic definition of public housing, but rather going into social housing which implies not only the brick and mortar but also the kind of community, equality, and integrated housing. It is much more socialistic than the minister would lead us to believe. I think there ought to be some scrutiny in this regard, the change from the traditional public funding by the federal government to a socialistic housing policy.
The area which is of most interest to me tonight is the change to a new era of financing proposed by Bill C-29, a shift from the funding which was hitherto the responsibility of the federal government. That responsibility for funding is now being shifted to the private sector. In effect, the private sector will take on the socialistic policies of the federal government. This is evident in two particular areas. One area is with regard to RRAP, which my colleague, the hon. member for Rosedale, will deal with, but I hope that the minister, being from the province of Quebec, realizes that with the large number of renters in that province it will be of particular concern to Quebeckers. No longer will the federal government provide funds for the RRAP program. They must now come exclusively from the private sector, which will bring hardship to the province of Quebec in particular because funding from the private sector will not come easy.
In the last year we have witnessed a fiasco in the AHOP program. My colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East, will be talking about AHOP, but certainly I want to deal with GPMs. GPMs are replacing the AHOP program, so we must look at AHOP to see what went wrong with it in order to determine whether GPMs can correct it.
AHOP was based on two premises, shaky as they were. I am surprised that the superminister, who at one time was minister

February 26, 1979
Housing
of urban affairs, even allowed AHOP to come into being. I applaud the government for innovative ideas, for new concepts, but it is foolhardy, it is stupid, it is irresponsible for a government to jump from one program into another without evaluating the First one. They are jumping from AHOP into GPMs without evaluating AHOP.
The two premises on which AHOP rested were, first, that the real disposal income of AHOP families would increase. The other day the minister said-and I cannot quote him exactly-"I am sorry that their incomes did not rise to their expectations; I am sorry that their real incomes did not go up as much as they had thought or hoped." He is sorry to bring in a program based on the fact that incomes would rise-then the government brought in wage and price controls which would negate that fact-but he introduces it after 10 per cent of AHOP units in this country are in default. That figure will double within four or five months.
AHOP was based on the assumption that the real value of the property would increase. We knew what happened to land and house prices at the turn of the decade, yet this government based a program on the expectation, upon the certainty, that real estate values would increase. In the last couple of years, sir, real estate has not appreciated. Now that the first five-year term is over we find that the value of AHOP homes has not escalated. Because of the subsidy against the second mortgage-held by CMHC or the lender-those two combined exceeded the value of the home. With the market interest rates of today and the real PIT doubled in many cases, we are faced with walk-aways and defaults.
In that setting the government turned its back on AHOP, still defending it in this House and across the country. If they could humble themselves for once and bring themselves to admit-the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo) is in the House tonight and this could easily be said of her-that they make a mistake in judgment, as we all do from time to time; if only they could come before the House and the Canadian people and say, "We made a mistake in judgment, we acted without the full facts," instead, they defend their actions today-and it will be to the death of this government.
Instead of admitting that AHOP is a colossal failure with massive defaults, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs stands in this House and defends it. But it is so good that he abandons the program and brings in GPM! That alone is evidence that the AHOP funding was inadequate, badly based, and irresponsible.
Let us examine the GPMs and see what the lending institutions say about this new government funding scheme. I shall only take time for two quotations. An article in the Free Press of February 21 reports an interview with Mr. M. L. Lahn of Canada Trust in which he said that most foreclosures of Canada Trust are related to the disastrous AHOP. The article goes on as follows:

Canada Trust became a lender under the AHOP program "most reluctantly and only in support of government policy." The loans were government insured, otherwise the company would not have participated, the president said.
The current Central Mortgage and Housing Corp. (CMHC) sponsored graduated payments loans almost ensure negative equities and even greater foreclosure problems unless inflation in housing values occurs rapidly-a rather inappropriate social premise on which to proceed.
He goes on to say that he will not participate. Perhaps the minister wants to pass off lightly what the trust companies say, but he cannot pass off the Royal Bank. Mr. W. Peter Carter, the general manager of mortgage services for the Royal Bank-he is no little teller, he is the man who is going to make the policy-was interviewed by The Tribune. An article which appeared in the February 17 issue reports in part as follows:
He said the GPM lending scheme is an example of both "irresponsible lending" and "irresponsible government."
The article went on to quote him as follows:
The major chartered banks have told Central Mortgage and Housing Corp. of our concerns and have told them bluntly that we are not prepared to promote such a scheme," he said. "We think it is morally indefensible."
The Royal Bank will not lend a nickel to the GPM. Last Friday, with the knowledge of the disaster of AHOP, with the knowledge that the lending institutions have told him the policy is wrong, indefensible, immoral and irresponsible, the minister said in this House, "Boys, we are going to go ahead anyway."
Sir, GPM could work. Here is a formula. The minister is in the House and he should take his pencil and write it down. The super minister is also here. He should write it down in case the Minister of State for Urban Affairs cannot understand it. Here is the formula by which GPMs could work.
Let us look at the government's proposal. It is for 5 per cent down and that the level of payments in the first five years be 75 per cent of the normal level of payments. That means that for the first nine years, in fact for the first 15 years, the debt against the house will exceed the original principal owing on the house. That will guarantee for the first 15 years that whoever owns it will owe more than they paid for the house. It will be negative equity. That is why the Royal Bank and Canada Trust have said they will not participate, because of that kind of irresponsible lending practice.
They have suggested that if the minister would use the formula of 14 per cent down, 14 per cent front end equity and 75 per cent of standard level payment, it would work. That would always ensure that the debt would never exceed the original principal, or cost of the house. Alternatively, they could put 8 per cent down and have the payments 85 per cent of the normal level payments. Either of those would work as long as at any given time there would be no negative equity. That is the key to making the GPM work. Any other formula will not work.
The minister knew this scheme was bound for disaster. The banks and financial institutions of the country as well as the CMHC warned him. He knew this would not be an exciting program to the banks because of the track record of AHOP. The GPM is identical to AHOP in the concept of 5 per cent and 75 per cent.
February 26, 1979

The minister must have thought that he could throw in a sweetener-give them a deal they could not refuse. In effect he told the private banking institutions, "The government is not going to have any more responsibility for funding for families whose incomes cannot buy a normal market mortgage." He was saying that the government is going to wipe its hands of funding responsibility and put it all in the private sector. He was saying, "Boys, here is a deal you cannot refuse. If you accept this kind of funding which has already proved to be disastrous in AHOP"-that is my editorial note-the minister did not admit that, never has, and probably never will. The sweetener is-and this is all in the bill-that if the GPMs are in default for 90 days, all the lender-the trust company or the bank-has to do is to phone CMHC and tell them, and CMHC says, "All right, we will make good the mortgage." It is done immediately, without any foreclosure procedure, without any normal period in which they can give notice of foreclosure to the tenant, or to the mortgagee. There is none of that. CMHC will pay up immediately. That was the sweetener, and knowing it was a bad economic policy the government said, "Do not worry, this will not cost you a cent. If they are three months in arrears, we will guarantee the payment."
Sir, I am glad that the banks and the trust companies in this country are more responsible than the minister. They said, "That kind of financing is morally indefensible. We will not do it. We will not go along with it." Here is the answer, sir. I will make those changes in committee. I will make the amendments that will change the GPMs so that they will be acceptable to the lending institutions of this country. I will give the minister notice now that if he does not accept those and the other amendments which we have proposed on this side to clean up Bill C-29 and make it look like a housing policy instead of political gimmickry, we will not support this bill on third reading. We will vote for it to go to committee so we can clean it up. That is the stance we are taking. It is a positive stance, getting ready for government.
We have positive proposals. We will take them to the committee and we will move every amendment necessary to make this act work and to make it equitable. We will make it do all the things the minister claims he wants done but claims he cannot because the legislation is inadequate. We will do that. But if you do not accept those, sir, we will vote against this bill on third reading. We will do so because the legislation is wrong and the GPM is morally indefensible. It will lead to the same kinds of disasters we have experienced with AHOP.
There are two other alternatives about which we have been talking. These are positive suggestions that we have asked the minister to consider in the area of housing. We have asked him to look at reverse annuities for senior citizens or for those people who have equity in their homes but may want to turn that equity into an annuity. We have asked the minister to look at that. Up to this point in time there have been no studies and no reviews. We have not had a minute's worth of study done by this minister's department on reverse annuities.
Housing
We have asked the minister to look at variable rates. But as soon as we say that variable rates are popular in some states of the United States, the minister has this phobia that interest deductibility is an American phenomenon. It is an American dream but it has been part of the American housing policy for some 50 years. So the minister has this phobia that an Americanized dream is something wrong. It is something like saying that we cannot copy those Americans. The minister has not even considered this suggestion. As a matter of fact, the words variable mortgage have never passed his lips. He cannot bring himself to say the words. We are saying the words tonight. I am asking the minister to look at variable rates in mortgages which have worked successfully in many of the states in the United States.
I see that my time has almost expired, but before closing I would like to tell the minister that we have been watching his activities over the last year. We have been waiting for this legislation. I want to tell you, sir, that I am disappointed that this minister continues hacking at the branches instead of digging at the roots. He hacks at the branches, changing the rules. He has a program one day which he changes the next. He has an AHOP policy one day and he abolishes it the next. This government, and this minister, will be known as the government of default by default. I would hope that when we take the reins of government the comparison will be made that they were the government of default and we were the government of no fault.
To that end we would commit ourselves and our party not only to good economic policy but to a housing policy of equity for all.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Miss Aideen Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the National Housing Act amendments which provide some needed additional flexibility. I am particularly pleased that the restrictions were removed from the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program so that it is no longer limited to housing in areas designated for neighbourhood improvement. When this bill is passed, the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, or RRAP, as most people know it, will make available to individual home owners CMHC direct loans and subsidies based on income. Co-operative housing groups and non-profit associations will also be eligible for RRAP assistance without being limited to designated areas.
Representing as I do an urban constituency with older housing and with many skilled construction workers who could do repairs and reconstruction, I am particularly pleased to see measures that favour renovation and preservation of older housing.
Many of our Canadian housing programs up to now have been aimed at increasing the supply of new houses. For example, ceilings on the AHOP program were such that, in Toronto, buyers were limited to a condominium or a townhouse in the suburbs. But many people prefer to live near their

February 26, 1979
Housing
families and friends in the inner city without having to spend a lot of time and money travelling to and from work, hence the importance of renovating older homes and doing this in a way which makes these homes accessible to people with low incomes, whether these older homes are renovated by individual home owners or by a group of people who have decided to form a co-operative in order to provide themselves with affordable housing.
Prior to 1973 co-operative housing was treated as just another form of home ownership and received the same treatment and benefits as a single applicant for a home owner loan. I am referring here to both types of housing co-operatives, first the building co-operatives in which a group of people simply pool their resources to build their housing at the same time with each member of the group owning a unit outright, to do with as she or he pleases, and second, the continuing co-operative or the non-profit group which provide housing for members, in which case the co-operative itself owns the housing, each member has a share in the project, and none of the units in such a co-operative can be sold for a profit.
By 1973, although building co-operatives received some assistance, continuing co-operatives under group ownership had great difficulty in getting recognition and acceptance under the act. One problem was that legislation did not provide for co-operatives to obtain loans for low rental housing, except as the sponsor for a project in which residents did not have to be members. In other words, people with low and moderate income could have housing provided for them, but they could not own it through a co-operative.
Another problem prior to 1973 was that co-operatives could obtain funding only for new projects, not for existing housing, nor even for the rehabilitation of existing housing. As a result, people in a rental project could not get an NHA loan to buy it co-operatively even if the landlord wished to sell it to them. This made it difficult indeed to mount a strong national progam of co-operative housing.
Nineteen seventy-three, however, saw the beginning of some of the changes, the final development of which we see in the present bill. This was aimed at helping co-operatives to develop fully as another housing alternative, and particularly for Canadians with low and moderate incomes. The two most important provisions in the 1973 legislation were, first, that housing co-operatives could qualify for 100 per cent loans for non-profit, low rental housing; and, second, loans were made available for both the purchase and rehabilitation of existing housing. That new legislation in effect started a new form of co-operatives, one in which members are collectively owners but individually are in a leasehold position. On the one hand, they have the proprietary rights of a landlord and, on the other hand, the rights and advantages of tenants.
Recently the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) had extensive discussions with the Co-Operative Housing Foundation of Canada which resulted in an agreement concerning the administration of subsidies and charges to occupants of the housing units that serve mutual objectives.
The new agreement provides for fewer controls by CMHC on actual project development, and allows co-operatives to have the opportunity to use a wider range of procurement techniques based on the group's experience. Greater latitude is also given to co-operative groups in choosing between the acquisition of existing developments and the construction of new projects. The agreement provides, as well, for a significant increase in the federal financial support to co-operative projects, and continued application of the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program. This agreement reflects the greater experience that has been gained in co-operative housing.
One important feature of the new legislation is that co-operative housing will be available to anyone, on a rent to income basis. Those who can afford to pay the full rent will do so. Those whose income is not sufficient to allow them to afford the full rent will pay according to their income, and the resulting losses will be offset by federal government subsidies.
There is no doubt that the new program will result in much higher production of this much needed type of accommodation; federal assistance will be almost doubled, and I understand that private lending institutions have indicated their willingness to invest as much as $500 million during the next few years in support of co-operative housing. This means that the number of people living in co-operative housing could easily double in a few years, going from the present level of about 50,000 to more than 100,000.
I am pleased to see this enhanced support to co-operative housing. It represents another means of offering an improved choice to families who want to own a home and are willing to put work into it but do not have large amounts of capital available.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see that the Minister of Public Works and Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) is in his place tonight. I know he has been following the debate very closely. I hope he will follow what I have to say.	.
First, I think this has to be said. It has been mentioned by other members in the debate. It seems we should have been dealing with this bill six months ago, if not a year ago. That would have given us an opportunity to give it the kind of scrutiny and the kind of committee study that it requires.
There are many good, very commendable features in the bill. Quite frankly, there are also parts of the bill that bother us. They require much closer scrutiny. Consequently we are looking for the opportunity of giving the bill, if the life of this parliament permits, the kind of scrutiny in committee that it so justly deserves and warrants, especially given the performance of this minister during his tenure as minister responsible for housing and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I wish to speak on one aspect of the bill, namely, the program that will replace the Assisted Home Ownership Program. There is no question about the commendable objectives

February 26, 1979

of the AHOP program. It has succeeded in making affordable housing available across this country to people who normally would not be able to afford to buy a home, especially in this inflationary period we are going through at the present time. It has succeeded in that objective.
Perhaps one of the reasons AHOP is in trouble, and it is in serious trouble notwithstanding the fact that it is about to be scrapped and replaced by a new program, is because it was put in place with unseemly haste. Projects were approved without due regard to the inspection capability of the corporation or of the Ministry of State for Housing and Urban Affairs.
What should have been a bonanza for the low income earners who could not afford housing has in fact turned out to be a bonanza in the form of a substantial windfall to some of the developers and builders in this country, some of whom set up fly by night operations merely to cash in on the government's haste to get on with the AHOP program.
One only has to go across this country and look at some of the projects that have been built under the program. I have seen several. In the city of Surrey, in the Vancouver area, there is an AHOP program which is disgraceful. I hope my colleague who represents that part of the country will enlarge upon that. I find the situation all across the country. Montreal has a substantial AHOP program with serious problems because of inadequate inspection, hasty construction, and the use of substandard building materials. The same is true in the city of Hamilton and in my own city of St. John's.
It is that program in the city of St. John's that I want to speak about tonight for a few moments. I do so because it happens to be in my constituency and because of the fact that I believe what has happened in the Virginia Park AHOP program is unfortunately typical of what has happened to other AHOP projects across the country. Let us take a look at it.
This project was built by a contractor who formed a special sub-company, if I can put it that way, to carry out this project. That company no longer exists. What does exist is over 100 houses on which the brick is deteriorating. Substandard building materials were used within and without. There is faulty plumbing, faulty wiring, inadequate insulation, indeed in places no insulation at all, all pointing to the fact that this project obviously did not receive adequate inspection.
As a result of some very good investigative reporting by the CBC program "The Fifth Estate", aired on December 5, there is now an RCMP investigation into allegations of pay-offs by the builder to CMHC inspectors. Charges have not been laid but the allegations have been made and the investigation is under way.
I first brought this matter to the attention of the minister almost two years ago. At that time the complaint did not relate to faulty brick as that had not made itself apparent. I was requested by the people who were buying these homes under the Assisted Home Ownership Program to inspect personally some of the grievances they were trying to get redressed by
Housing
CMHC. I saw first hand in these houses the use of bathroom fixtures that, at best, could only be described as seconds. For example, one thing I noticed in several of the houses I visited was that the bath tubs had cracks in them. I asked the home owner who first identified this what excuse he had been given for this. He said he had been told that one of the workmen had dropped a hammer into the bath tub. I found that this workman had dropped several hammers in that particular block because every second or third house I examined had a bath tub with a crack in it. Similarly with the sink fixtures, they were just hanging from the walls.
There was inadequate plastering and the windows dit not fit, to the point that on a rainy day with the wind blowing in a certain direction the rain would come inside the house. There were problems in relation to inadequate insulation resulting in unusually high heating bills. All these things were identified in that project several years ago. Letters were written, but nothing was done about them. It took the deterioration of substandard brick to bring this matter to a head.
When this bill does get before committee I will have the opportunity to lay the whole sordid picture of the Virginia Park AHOP project before this House in the form of photographs, affidavits, engineering studies and the whole bit.
What I and these people find difficult to understand is the attitude of the minister and of CMHC. This matter has been raised on a number of occasions in the House by myself, and the response from the minister has been to the effect that this is not the responsibility of CMHC. What was their response when confronted with this? Their response was that they would make additional moneys available to the owners of these houses so they could carry out the necessary repairs themselves. On the face of it that seemed like a reasonable offer, until it was discovered that what they intended to do was make the additional moneys available to the home owners and then add it on to their mortgages, giving them a year or two before they had to start paying back the additional moneys. In addition, they would have to pay back an unfixed interest rate on the money for that period of time during which payments were not made. That was the generous offer the minister made.
In reply to my question of January 23, the minister said as reported at page 2440 of Hansard'.
The offer does not only include an increase in the loan, but the possibility of subsidies attached to this offer of an extra loan in order to allow people to make urgent repairs to their homes. Discussions are going on at the present time between the CMHC regional director and the lawyer representing some of the owners, but I should like the people concerned to look fully at the advantages which are offered, because CMHC is going beyond normal practice in trying to accommodate them and help them solve their problems.
These are not their problems because, unless the minister comes to his senses, or a case can be made in committee following which the minister adopts a more reasonable and positive attitude, this will be a question for the courts to decide.
What we are looking at here is a project in respect of which CMHC approved the builder in the first instance. CMHC had to approve the site and approve the plans of the buildings. It

February 26, 1979
Housing
had to approve the materials that were being used, and had to inspect the construction throughout, and in fact make the final inspection before making progress payments available to the contractor. That all took place before the home owners came into the picture, so there is no question about where responsibility lies.
Although the minister has not told me this, has not said so in the House, the reason the minister and CMHC have taken this attitude toward the Virginia Park AHOP project is that they are afraid of opening the flood gates. They know there are literally hundreds and hundreds of AHOP houses across this country which people bought from CMHC in good faith, secure at the time in the knowledge that they had been inspected by the national housing agency of the Government of Canada and approved by that agency. They felt they had a reasonably good investment, but found when they moved in that the houses had been inadequately inspected. That is the only logical conclusion you can come to after examining these projects, not just Virginia Park. You must come to the conclusion that in fact somebody had failed to ensure adequately through the inspection process that first class materials were being used throughout.
CMHC has now taken the attitude that these people have to assume the financial responsibility for this faulty brick, for the inadequate or substandard building materials, and for the inspectors who must have been blindfolded when they inspected and approved some of these things I saw first-hand. These people are expected now to pay for the mistakes of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs and for the mistakes of CMHC. Can you imagine the minister and CMHC now saying these people who have had their problems fully identified by the National Research Council, which did a study of the brick, and by professionals who were readily able to identify some of the serious flaws in construction and some of the substandard materials used, are themselves responsible? Can you imagine them saying they will provide the funds necessary to make the repairs but will add them on to the mortgages? They will not indicate what interest they will have to pay on that money until a year or two down the road. In the interim they will get the money that will be added to their mortgages and will have to pay interest for the use of that money.
These people have unanimously rejected that offer outright. There was not one single dissenting voice to that rejection. There was no political coercion, because they spoke through their solicitor, a gentleman by the way who has been doing a first-class job on behalf of these people notwithstanding that at one point in time he was a Liberal candidate in St. John's
East. He has been doing a first class job for these people, without any remuneration whatsoever. There is no political motivation behind what has been happening at Virginia Park, but each time this question has been raised in the House the minister has admitted that a problem exists. He has also been very quick to admit that in no way could the corporation be considered financially liable for what has happened to these homes. What has happened to them?
My colleague, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway), has referred to the fact that many of these homes have depreciated in value, partly because of the fact that the housing market has levelled off, but largely because of the fact that many of them were built, all at the same price, and held at a certain level. Let us say I am in the city of Toronto and I pay $45,000 for my house. Someone moves in next year and pays $45,000 for his house, so the price of my house remains the same. These houses have depreciated in value because of faulty construction and substandard materials, yet the minister and CMHC fully expect these people to add on to their financial liability and to increase the cost of houses which have in fact depreciated in value. It is not difficult to understand why such an offer was rejected, if it can be dignified by being termed an offer.
The offer was rejected outright. I am not concerned about the flood gates. I am not concerned about the fact that the minister may very well be setting a precedent if he decides to deal with Virginia Park in a just way. He may be setting a precedent he will have to live with in Montreal, in Hamilton, in Vancouver, or wherever this problem, which seems to be characteristic of AHOP across the country, occurs. I am concerned only with seeing that justice is done for those people who bought those houses having faith in National Housing Act inspections and through the good offices and because of the good reputation of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I look forward to confronting the minister when this matter goes to committee. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take the floor on this important piece of legislation concerning our population's most urgent needs.
If I may, I would first like to comment on the speech just made by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). To me, he seemed more like a housing inspector than a legislator. He mentioned a few isolated cases of possibly inadequate construction, but he once more reflected his party's attitude; as far as construction is concerned, his party has barely reached the plumbing phase, whereas the Liberal party is into urban planning.
The attitude shown by the hon. member who preceded me exactly reflects the position of a party lacking in imagination, except to limit itself by telling Canadians: Ask your municipalities to increase your municipal taxes and we will give you a $2 billion federal income tax credit.
Mr. Speaker, this is applying a band-aid where a review of the planning process is needed. I am proud to belong to a party which has improved the construction situation in this country; the picture is highly positive when one considers that an average of 250,000 units have been built in Canada the last four years. We note that, from 1967 to 1977, we have, through the federal housing agency, built a great number of housing units-an average of 10 new units per 1,000 inhabitants.
I would like to take this opportunity to thank the ministers responsible whom I see here tonight: the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers, the hon. member from Thunder Bay and also the hon. member for Papineau, the present Minister of Public Works, who were largely responsible for these initiatives and achievements in housing. I think that in the eyes of Canadians these figures and these achievements are much more serious and positive guarantees for the future than the speech made by the hon. member for St. John's East, where he dealt with specific cases out of the number of housing units in Canada that I mentioned. He preferred to speak of local problems rather than deal with this issue to the extent covered in the legislation before us.
The purpose of this bill, Mr. Speaker, once the provinces have been consulted, is to adopt a global approach to federal financial assistance to municipalities by combining the neighbourhood improvement program, the municipal infrastructure program and the municipal grants program in a single community services grant program. One of the objectives, and certainly not the least, in view of the present housing situation for low
Housing
income earners and the fact that under existing agreements we are building 19,000 housing units, is to build 30,000 such units for low income earners.
The federal and provincial governments agreed to finance those three programs to the extent of $150 million for 1979, $250 million for 1980 that will be distributed at the provincial level through community services contributions based on the population and the financial capacities of the municipalities.
For the information of hon. members and particularly the people who are listening and watching us, the province of Newfoundland will get through this new legislation $4.2 million in 1979 and $7 million in 1980. As concerns the province of Quebec, it will get about $47 million for 1979, and $78 million for 1980. I shall not list the amounts for each province but it is clearly mentioned in the legislation.
Mr. Speaker, I am very optimistic as concerns our performance in the housing field, and the infrastructure at the municipal level, and as the hon. member for Laval, which is the second largest municipality in the province of Quebec, in population and area, I can say that we benefited from the help given by the Canadian government to all those programs. I think that as concerns the population of Laval, I must congratulate the Canadian government and the minister responsible, who is now Minister of Public Works, for the precious contribution we got through those various programs, the social housing program, the infrastructure program or the municipal assistance program, to allow municipalities to make the most economical possible use of the land for building projects in view of the increasing cost of public utilities. As an example, the amount of $2,157,000 was given to the city of Laval under this assistance program for municipalities which want to build in high density residential areas. If we take this amount and relate it to general rates, this meant a reduction of 3 per cent in general rates for all residents in the city of Laval in 1976-77 and will probably mean the same thing this year. If we take a house assessed at $40,000, this means $120 per home owner under the policy which was cancelled last December.
Even though I am quite optimistic about this program and the results obtained by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, I am much more concerned about this bill, as I told the minister when he appeared before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. I expressed my concern while being well aware that this was a request made by the provinces under the pretext that it come under provincial or municipal jurisdiction, which is quite true, but we have accepted that this become more and more a provincial responsibility, and the various projects will be approved following applications made by the provinces.

February 26, 1979
Adjournment Debate
Let us look at the situation of social housing in 1977. Mr. Speaker, I refer you to the annual report of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. We can read the following on page 20, and this describes in summary the interest shown by the provinces in the development of social housing. The House will see how my concern is justified if we take into account what I have just mentioned. This is what it says:
The largest shortfall in loan commitments under CMHC's 1977 capital budget was for the construction and acquisition of housing for low and moderate income people. This was particularly marked for public housing to be rented to tenants according to an approved rent-to-income scale. Commitments for this type of housing financed with loans by CMHC to the provinces, and by joint investment undertakings by CMHC and the provinces, totalled only $199 million in 1977 compared to a budget allocation for the year of $353 million.
-which means that $199 million of the $353 million available were used, and I continue:
In 1976, some $403 million had been committed for these purposes under the National Housing Act.
So we can definitely see a rather considerable reduction in the amounts which were made available to the provinces for public housing. I bring to the attention of all provinces and of all organizations that if this amendment is made through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act, we shall reach our objectives, namely to increase the number of housing units for low income people.

subtopic: AIRPORTS-NAVIGATIONAL AIDS AND FIREFIGHTING EQUIPMENT FOR CASTLEGAR, B.C.
AIRPORTS-NAVIGATIONAL AIDS AND FIREFIGHTING EQUIPMENT FOR CASTLEGAR, B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 20 I addressed two questions to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) relative to the firefighting equipment at Castlegar and the navigational aids at Castlegar airport. In his response the minister made what I consider to be an innocent mistake, one which I drew to his attention as a point of order a couple of days ago. Whereas I was talking about third party contract agreements, the minister was under the impression that I was directing my question to the subject of insurance contracts for smaller airports across the country.

I am well aware of the fact there are a number of smaller airports across Canada which were concerned about this particular problem, and that the minister covered some 37 airports with a $100 million liability insurance per airport. In itself that action has taken a great deal of strain off the concerns of the smaller regional municipal airports. The minister failed to understand in my question that I was referring to third party contracts, the habit of the government to turn over the operation of regional airports to a third party. There are a couple of classic examples.
I suggest Your Honour should look at Resolute Bay where, in a period of a few years, there was a 229 per cent increase in the operational costs of the airport. Also we can look at the record of Frobisher Bay operated by the Tower Corporation out of Montreal. We will see that Nordair and its pilots expressed considerable dissatisfaction over the operation of that field. We see in a very remote area an airport which recently was blocked completely from any contact with the outside world through that travel mode by virtue of several days of blizzard. We see an airport which does not have a fire chief and does not have the type of firefighting expertise one would expect to be in place in an airport with such a remote location.
When the briefing session was held for the people bidding on the third party contract for Castlegar airport, it was interesting to note that some of the bidding parties did not even know where Castlegar was located. Some had mistaken Cranbrook for Castlegar. Some thought it was somewhere in the northern part of the province. Others did not know where it was. There were three firms in Castlegar which bid on the operation of that airport. Although I am not fully convinced the third party operation is the route to go, certainly I would prefer being in a position to deal with a local contractor. But on the basis of the bids submitted, it appears the award may well go to Agda Ltd., a firm of consulting engineers in Ottawa. It could go to the second highest bidder, the Tower Corporation of Montreal. I think my suspicions will be borne out in fact. I suspect that any of these firms removed from the city of Castlegar will have that operation run by subcontractors. Not only do we see the operation of the airport run at arm's length or at some considerable distance, also we see subcontractors running the airport. The service at that airport will deteriorate as a result of this kind of nonsense.
In terms of the navigational aids which I raised with the minister, and in terms of firefighting equipment, Castlegar has received nothing but empty promises. They were promised a foam truck over a year ago. They still have no foam truck and no facilities for storing it in the winter, as foam freezes.
Castlegar was promised a new navigational aid to replace the one which comes out of the Smithsonian Institute located at Crescent Valley, a navigational aid which is so old that the ministry has trouble finding spare parts for that particular unit. Yet these promises have not borne fruit.
February 26, 1979

We find that the Ministry of Transport denied Castlegar airport the construction of a sand shed so that the sand would not freeze. They said that it would be too expensive, so it was taken out of the airport budget, and the workers themselves at the airport built it, solidly, for $6,000. We find that Kelowna has an aluminum frame building which is sitting there and getting mouldy with age. This building sat there for a year and nobody knew who ordered it, why it was ordered or what it was to be used for. Yet it was there, but there was nothing for Castlegar. Penticton has 61 employees under the Ministry of Transport, but Castlegar has less than half that.
In terms of navigational aids the minister has said that he is concerned that they use navigational aids according to the geographical conditions of that particular area. No other airport in Canada is more qualified for a VOR than Castlegar. The approaches to Castlegar are exceedingly narrow. It does not qualify under any of today's terms of instrument landing technology for instrument landing. Therefore it is time that Castlegar received a VOR and that the minister stopped fooling the public.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIRPORTS-NAVIGATIONAL AIDS AND FIREFIGHTING EQUIPMENT FOR CASTLEGAR, B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to provide a brief bit of background information in response to the question by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco), dealing with firefighting equipment and navigational aids for the airport at Castlegar.
A contract operation of the airport has become necessary because of a decision made by the city of Castlegar to cease operating the airport effective March 31 of this year. The city has been fully consulted with regard to this course of action. Other possible, but less favourable, options would have been the closure of the airport or operation by Transport Canada.
It is planned, Mr. Speaker, to place a small foam crash truck capable of carrying 400 gallons into Castlegar airport around the middle of April this year. This vehicle will remain in Castlegar until such time as deliveries of medium foam trucks, capable of carrying 1,000 gallons, commence from the next contract. The next contract for airport emergency vehicles is in the tendering stage at the present time, and one medium foam truck for Castlegar is included.
The "D" category airport in which Castlegar falls requires a first response truck and a foam truck of 850 gallons capacity. Castlegar already has a first response truck. With the addition of the small foam truck of 400 gallons, it will be slightly deficient in the amount of water carried during the interim pending arrival of the new medium foam truck of 1,000 gallons.

In August 1978, the installation of a localizer beacon with distance measuring equipment, commonly called DME, in Castlegar was approved and the project was to be carried out in 1982-83. Since then, Mr. Speaker, it has become possible to carry out that project in 1980-81.
Adjournment Debate
Such equipment will replace the low-frequency range used in Castlegar and will provide better signals to pilots making ILS approaches. In addition, DME facilities on the ground will give a more accurate distance between aircraft and airport to planes equipped with that device. The information provided by both navigational aids will give the pilot a better position reading during the ILS approach, which is an improvement to the navigational aid system of that airport.

subtopic: FISHERIES-NEGOTIATIONS RESPECTING ALASKA COAST HALIBUT FISHERY
FISHERIES-NEGOTIATIONS RESPECTING ALASKA COAST HALIBUT FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 20 I rose in the House to ask the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) the following questions'.
What is the status of negotiations relative to halibut fishing off the Alaska coast?
And, secondly, I stated:
-the fishermen in that area are very concerned that their privileges will be exchanged for rights granted in eastern waters. They have registered their protest with the minister with respect to this matter. Reports are that they will be excluded from American waters and they will have to go to Canadian waters which are already overfished.
There are at least four areas of concern, and possibly more, which the fishermen in British Columbia have. I raised the matter in the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry just a few days ago, but I did not get much more satisfaction from the minister at that time than I have received in this House.
In committee I discovered that the United States government served notice on the Minister of Fisheries several years ago that they were planning to end the halibut fishing convention which has been in operation for something like 55 years off the cost of Alaska. If the minister knew two years ago that there was going to be some finality to this agreement, why did we not have a fallback position? Was there no back-up position for our negotiators when they went to Juneau to negotiate last September?
The second important question is: what happens to the halibut fishermen during this time? The negotiated settlement with the United States provides that this year Canadian halibut fishermen will be able to catch half of their normal catch quota, and next year it will be one quarter of their normal catch quota. A fisherman who is handed an ultimatum that he can only catch half as much as in other years would begin to worry about his income, especially if he has a boat with a crew of four or five to look after. He must wonder how he is to make a living. There are from 40 to 60 craft with a total crew of up to 250 people who must wonder what they will be doing this summer. If that is to be the normal catch, half of them must be wondering, and the rest will have to wonder after next year. If we consider the gross products involved in
80050 - 15

February 26, 1979
Adjournment Debate
Canadian export, then we must worry because there is no other market for them at the present time.
The next problem is one of confidence. The halibut fishermen are organized into about nine different groups. All were invited to go with Ambassador Cadieux to help negotiate the settlement. After the negotiations were settled they sent a news release to the minister saying unanimously, "We are opposed to this agreement because we cannot make a living with this kind of settlement." I grant that one person did not sign because the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo) called him directly and asked him not to sign. The rest of them all signed as being opposed. They would rather have settled for three million pounds than the two million and be cut off entirely next year, than get the kind of half life settlement they are subject to this time.
Regardless of what the fishermen wanted, Mr. Cadieux accepted it. I cannot help but wonder why they were invited in the first place. If people who know something about the industry first hand, unanimously rejected the agreement, then what was the ambassador trying to do?
My fourth concern is about what will happen to the ground-fishermen off the coast of Vancouver Island. In committee the other day the minister admitted that those stocks are already at a critical stage of depletion and that we cannot afford to fish them much more extensively than at the present. Surely the United States fishermen in the area are going to get all they can from those fishing grounds. I wonder about the kind of surveillance the Department of Fisheries has been exercising when our stock cannot reach that state. We have something like 140 trawlers out there working those fishing grounds which are at a critical level already. What happens if 40 or 60 halibut fishermen are introduced to the area? The United States fishermen who are withdrawing will be replaced by Canadian fishermen coming into the area.
Finally, there is one more concern that I need to put on the record. That is the presence of factory ships. The minister has introduced licences. He says all the time that these are for stocks that Canadians are not accustomed to fishing and processing. That may be true, but that does not mean that they are not doing it. With the kind of surveillance that we have in that area, I question whether that Polish ship, or whatever flag it is flying, is restricted to that kind of a licence.
I asked the minister a very pointed question in the lobby several weeks ago. He had his executive assistant with him at that time. My question was: what kind of a labour agreement does that factory ship have because the fishermen in B.C. are wondering about it. It was a secret negotiation, apparently. The minister turned to his assistant and asked him to find out and to let me know. To this day I have not heard what kind of an agreement or contract it was. Those fish are being caught out there, they are being processed and transported out there, but the Canadian economy gets no tax benefit and apparently little labour benefit from it. Canadian people, and certainly the fishermen on the west coast, have a right to know what

kind of an agreement has existed between the factory ship- that flag ship-and the Government of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Pearsall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: FISHERIES-NEGOTIATIONS RESPECTING ALASKA COAST HALIBUT FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, negotiations between Canada and the U.S.A. concerning Canadian halibut fishing off Alaska took place in Juneau, Alaska, February 14 and 15, and a proposed agreement was worked out. It has not, and I wish to emphasize at this time that it has not been approved by the two governments. The Canadian and the U.S. negotiators have made recommendations to their respective governments that, if approved, would mean the continuation of the International Pacific Halibut Commission and the phaseout of Canadian halibut fishing off Alaska.
Under the proposed agreement, Canadian fishermen would be allowed to catch two million pounds of halibut off Alaska in 1979 and one million pounds in 1980. In other words, compared to what Canadian fishermen took in 1978, they would be allowed to take about 55 per cent of that amount in 1979 and about 30 per cent in 1980. The two negotiators have also agreed to recommend that U.S. vessels be allowed to catch 3,250 metric tonnes of groundfish off British Columbia in 1979 and 1980, or about 40 per cent of recent levels.
I would like to point out that the Canadian halibut fishery that was under discussion was carried out in waters under the fisheries jurisdiction of the U.S.A., and if an agreement were not concluded, Canadian fishermen would not be allowed, and I repeat would not be allowed to fish for halibut in 1979 or subsequent years.
I would also like to reaffirm a statement made by the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) in the House on February 19, that if there is to be dislocation of the Canadian halibut fleet, a program of relocation is being considered. Officials have interviewed almost all of the owners of vessels which have fished in that area, and a program is being designed that will take into account the individual circumstances of the fishermen affected either by an abrupt termination of the Alaskan halibut fishery, or through a phase-out.

subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-SALES TAX ON STORM WINDOWS AND DOORS
NATIONAL REVENUE-SALES TAX ON STORM WINDOWS AND DOORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in the hope of obtaining a sensible answer to a question I put to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Abbott) on Tuesday, February 20. It concerns energy conservation in the home. It specifically relates to the government's decision in the November 16 budget to reimpose the 5 per cent federal sales tax on storm windows and doors. These are items which heretofore had been tax exempt.
I have received a communication from a manufacturer in St. Boniface who is in the door and window business. He is a small manufacturer and employs about 60 people. This is a very important industry in St. Boniface. In a telegram to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), my constituent stated:
February 26, 1979

Your reimposition of the federal sales tax on windows and door defeats discriminately our purpose in reducing energy wastage in this world energy crisis. You have deflated us and left us cold. We now see no purpose in pursuing the critical need to manufacture good double and triple windows to save energy. If every house in Canada was supplied with single windows then perhaps you would realize the importance of good windows and doors in this energy crisis. It is unfortunate that with the stroke of a pen and without any consultation with our industry you elected to penalize particularly the people in the cold west.
I ask the minister to explain the rationale behind this change in tax policy. In all fairness I should mention that the minister has made a stab at an explanation in a letter sent to my office on December 13. In that letter the minister explained, in a bewildering example of logic, that:
The exemption for storm doors and storm windows was originally intended to be confined to these goods for installation on existing buildings. This was not found to be practicable, however, and as a result, all double glass windows and glass cladding material became exempt from sales tax. As glass is less efficient in energy conservation than solid wall construction, the exemption did not achieve its original intent.
The government has made a point of professing its support for measures which would conserve energy. I wish to quote one short paragraph by a scientist with the Economic Council of Canada:
The implementation of energy conservation programs will benefit Canada more in both the short term and the long term than equivalent investments in new energy producing facilities, according to a paper by D. B. Brooks.
The government has encouraged Canadians to turn unnecessary lights off, to put on a sweater before adjusting the thermostat. Indeed, considerable lip service has been paid to saving energy. The government claimed the need to create an energy conscious atmosphere in Canada, with the idea that reduced consumption of energy would result in reduced dependence on imported oil. It is a worth-while and necessary pursuit. The energy crunch has everyone concerned. Only last week the government introduced legislation enabling it to ration energy supplies in case of emergency.
Conservation is a vital part of any national energy strategy. As we seek out new, more reliable sources of supply, we should also be working simultaneously to bring in measures which encourage more efficient use of energy. The reimposition of sales tax on storm windows and storm doors, as well as the continued taxation of insulated steel, one door systems, is lamentably misplaced, in that it acts to discourage efficient use of energy. There had been a good reason for the previous tax exemption on these items, namely, that double and triple glass storm windows and doors make a substantial contribution to the conservation of energy in the home. Now, because the minister has surmised that "glass is less efficient in energy conservation than solid wall construction", storm windows and doors are to be taxed. I really wonder if the minister expects us to live in houses with no windows? Of course glass is less energy efficient than solid walls, but double and triple glass is a lot more efficient than single glass.
Another concern arising from that confused letter is the distinction the minister makes between the need to encourage installation of energy efficient windows and doors on existing buildings and an apparent disinclination to provide for the
Adjournment Debate
inclusion of these same items on new buildings. Should not all buildings be equipped to conserve as much energy as much as possible?
I sincerely hope this government is interested in providing incentives for the conservation of energy. In the United States, not only is there a tax exemption on the sale of storm windows and doors, but a tax credit of 15 per cent is available for their installation. Somehow U.S. taxation officials in all their wisdom are able to get around the obstacles which dumbfound our government in its purported efforts to promote energy conservation in the home.
In Canada as well there has been recognition of the energy conservation value of double and triple glazed windows and doors. The Associate Committee of the National Building Code, of the National Research Council, determined in 1978 that within certain specifications double and triple glazing of windows or single glazing with a storm sash provide the necessary thermal resistance to be considered energy efficient. I wish we could make the government realize the value of insulated windows. We would like to see a co-ordinated energy conservation strategy put in place.

speakeroldname: Mr. Yves Demers (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue and Minister of State (Small Business)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-SALES TAX ON STORM WINDOWS AND DOORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the June 23, 1975 budget was brought down, the hon. John Turner announced three important changes in the excise and sales tax. Those changes included an exemption for storm windows, storm doors and double glass windows to be installed on existing buildings. The purpose of that exemption was to encourage the owners of those buildings to conserve energy.
It was realized that those double glass windows were being used not only on existing buildings but also in the construction of new ones. The use of those windows in the latter case was giving a fiscal advantage to the users of glass over the users of other conventional materials. The latter usually have to pay a tax at the reduced rate of 5 per cent. Let me give you as an example in the national capital: the Place du Portage buildings are built of pre-stressed concrete, which is subject to a rate of 5 per cent, while the Bank of Canada building, whose outside face is made of glass, is consequently tax exempt.
The June 1975 budget provided an exemption for that glass when used on existing buildings but not on new ones. It proved to be very difficult to apply the act, the manufacturer being unable to control the use of his products. Mostly because of that administrative difficulty, it was decided to cancel that

February 26, 1979

exemption in the November 16, 1978, budget. That is why, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Abbott) gave the answer he did in his letter of December 13 to the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Hare).
